subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When I moved the adjournment of the debate on Friday night, I did so in the hope that my hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Hatfield) rather than myself would speak to-day, and I feel that the House would prefer to hear that hon. gentleman. I sincerely trust, however, that at some future time we may have the pleasure of hearing him. Now, inasmuch as only one side of the case has been presented from the province in which I have the honour to represent a constituency, and lest the people of that province in common with the members of this House should think that the representatives of Prince Edward Island are all of one opinion in regard to the budget which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) has brought down on this occasion, I shall ask the indulgence of the House while I present the views of those people as I understand them. Before I proceed to discuss the budget, however, I beg to be allowed to welcome back to the House the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) who unfortunately has been absent through illness.
I am sure that all sides, irrespective of party, are glad to see him once more in the House.
I think I may also say on behalf of hon. members on this side that we shall all be only too pleased to welcome back, when he returns, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) who, I understand, has been slightly indisposed for the past few days. I for one admire our public men, whatever party they may represent. I have admiration for the leader of the opposition and respect for his followers, not only those who occupy the front benches but the members of that party generally. Naturally, too, I admire the,members of my own party, and before I resume my seat I shall probably have something further to say on that point.
As it is always a pleasure for one to be able to bring good news, I think the position in which the Minister of Finance found himself on April 15, when he was able to present to the House the budget now under consideration, must have been very gratifying indeed. Not only must it have been a matter for congratulation on the part of the minister himself, but it must have afforded the people of this Dominion from coast to coast an unusual degree of satisfaction to have such a budget brought down in this parliament. Our friends opposite tried, of course, as one would naturally expect an opposition to do, to criticize the budget adversely but I think the House will agree with me when I say that this criticism has not been characterized by any note of seriousness. The tidings which the Minister of Finance was able to broadcast to the people of Canada a month ago were of such a character that they must have been received with enthusiasm by hon. gentlemen opposite themselves. When for some fancied reason people fear that some dreadful pall is hanging over them, that some dire calamity
3408	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. MacLean (Prince)
is about to befall them, it is doubly gratifying to them to find that after all their fears were unfounded, that the storm that threatened has passed, and that the sun will dhine with increasing brightness, dispelling the gloom.
Hon. gentlemen opposite, though perhaps unintentionally, have painted a gloomy picture to the people of Canada. They have tried to tell the people, or at least some of the people, that if this dreadful alliance between Progressives and Grits continued the country would certainly be ruined. Those hon. gentlemen must have been greatly disappointed when the Minister of Finance was able to show that the Dominion had been able not only to meet all obligations but to report a surplus of over $20,000,000, besides reducing the income tax and in other ways lightening the burden of the people. In view of this satisfactory condition of affairs, my task to-day is a comparatively easy one. I do not think it requires any special pleading to convince a man that it is easier for him to pay $30 instead of $100 in income tax, nor is it difficult to prove to him that he can much more readily afford an automobile which costs to-day $150 less than it did previously. I do not think, either, that it calls for any special pleading to convince the people of this country that the return to the two-cent postage rate will benefit them at the same time increasing the revenues of the country as we hope it will. Contrary to the views expressed by some of our friends across the way, I firmly believe -we shall see an increase in the sales of automobiles, an increase in our postage revenue, and if not an increase at least a very slight falling off in our income tax revenue. Taking the revenue as a whole, I hope the next budget statement will show that the various reductions announced by the Minister of Finance this session have not materially affected it.
My good friend from Fort William (Mr. Manion) has moved an amendment to the budget. However its real intent may be camouflaged, I would draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, most emphatically to the fact that the hon. gentleman's amendment constitutes a direct vote against the budget in every particular. It is a direct vote against the reduction in the income tax; it is a direct vote against the reduction in the automobile duty; it is a direct vote against the return to penny postage; it is a direct vote against the wiping out of the receipt tax-in fact it is, I repeat, a direct vote against the budget as a whole. I do not think I need labour that point any further. Our friends opposite camouflage their opposition to the reduction in the automobile duties by saying: Leave

that to the tariff board. I venture the assertion, Mr. Speaker, that if the tariff board has recommended such a reduction, our friends across the way would immediately have condemned the tariff board and declared: This is something that the government should handle themselves and not leave to the tariff or any other board. In a word, they would have found some excuse for voting against the budget..
Although these hon. gentlemen have to a certain extent opposed the legislation that has been brought down, such as the bill for the revaluation of soldier settlers' land, the old age pensions bill and the rural credits bill, I am certain that they will not have the courage to vote against the final passage of any of these measures. I think I am safe in saying that they will sit absolutely quiet and swallow every bit of legislation when it comes up for third reading.

speechtext:
I feel sure that
in the course of a few days when the measures I have referred to come up for final disposition my prediction as to what will happen will be fully borne out.
Now, a great deal has been said by hon. gentlemen opposite about the pledges that they allege the Liberal government have broken during the past four years. We have been told that every pledge made to the people in 1921 has since been broken by the government. I take very strong exception to this allegation. In the 1921 election the big question before the electorate was: Will we be able to make revenue and expenditure meet? The Liberals said: Give us a chance and we will do it. They have accomplished this, as I shall show in a few minutes. They also promised to reduce the tariff on the implements of production. I submit, Sir, that this pledge has been fully redeemed. I remember quite well in the first two sessions of the last parliament hon. gentlemen opposite day after day taunted the government wtih having succeeded to office on the strength of these pledges: To reduce the tariff, and to make revenue and expenditure meet. We

The Budget-Mr. MacLean (Prince)
were told that the government had accomplished nothing towards the redemption of these pledges, that they were standing still, in fact they were afraid to make a move to implement those promises. Immediately the tariff reductions were made our friends opposite changed their tune and declared that we had ruined every factory throughout the Dominion. I state most emphatically, Mr. Speaker, that the pledges made to the people in 1921 by the Liberal party have since been fulfilled by this government. We have made revenue and expenditure meet, we have reduced the tariff on implements of productoin, and also the duties on certain commodities. The ruin that our friends opposite predicted would follow reduction of the protection enjoyed by the manufacturers of agricultural implements did not follow; on the contraiy, instead of driving our implement manufacturers out of business, their financial statements disclose that they have been making more money than they ever made under the former tariff. Our friends of the opposition are not now charging this government with doing nothing, they are not charging us with breaking our pledges, except in one particular. They claim that the Prime Minister pledged himself at the opening of parliament not to interfere with the tariff. Well, Sir, I do not think that the Speech from the Throne can be fairly construed as constituting such a pledge, nor do I agree that either the government or the Liberal party were in any way committed to the course suggested by our friends opposite.
Now, Mr. Speaker. I wish for a few minutes to deal with the financial condition of the country in an endeavour to prove to the House and to the people that we have met our pledges with respect to making revenue and expenditure meet. In this connection I propose to put a few figures on Hansard The gross national debt reached its peak in 1921. The public records show a reduction in 1925 of $84,000,000. The net national debt reached its peak in 1923. The public recards show a reduction of $4,698,116 for 1925, and a further reduction of $22,353,000 by this budget. In other words, there has been a reduction in the net debt of over $27,000,000. These figures are from the public records and can be verified by any hon. gentleman. They wil be found at page 46 of the Public Accounts. Sir, we have more than met that pledge to make the national revenues and expenditures balance, we have placed on the right side of the ledger a substantial surplus in reduction of the national debt.
But let me go a little further. Since confederation we have had only eleven surpluses
totalling $101,000,000; of these this government has to its credit a total of $58,692,182, made up of three surpluses as follows: 1924, $35,993,593; 1925, $345,589; 1926, $22,353,000. This government has been able to show a surplus greater by $15,602,277 than the surpluses shown by all governments from confederation to the present day. That is a record of which we on this side of the House should be extremely proud. We have been twitted by hon. members opposite since 1921 with our supposed inability to make revenues and expenditures meet, but these records prove the contrary. I do not think we need more substantial evidence of the progress made by this government in meeting its obligations and keeping its promises in this regard.
It has been stated1 that a large portion of our expenditure is uncontrollable, and I think that is perfectly true. It is very hard under present conditions for any government to show a substantial reduction in yearly expenditures. We have such large amounts as our provincial subsidies, aggregating over $12,000,000; interest on war debt amounting to $167,000,000; interest on debts other than war debt of over $12,000,000; pensions of over $36,000,0000 and superannuations of over $1,600,000. These are fixed charges which no government can escape; so long as Canada is a self-governing country these obligations must be met yearly, and it is impossible to make any substantial reductions in these amounts. I could make further reference to these matters but I think it is not necessary, because I feel sure the people in general are quite aware that this government has made revenue and expenditure meet. Not only that, but it is substantially reducing the debt, and everyone knows that Canada has turned the corner so far as her financial obligations are concerned.
The hon. member for Fort William in his speech the other day attributed a great deal to Providence; he said that Providence had been kind to this government and that by the assistance of Providence they were able to show a surplus. If that is so, Mr. Speaker, I must say that Providence was very unkind to the last administration, because never in the history of the Dominion has such a continuation of deficits been rolled up as was done by the late government. I therefore think I am safe in saying that, if the surplus Shown by this government is attributable to a kind Providence, that Providence was certainlv unkind to hon. members opposite when they were in office. On the other hand the hon. member said that Providence was kind to drunken men, and often took care of those in an intoxicated condition when they were not able to take care of themselves, alluding to the

Our finances would have been in much better shape, because the situation was certainly serious when this government came into power and there has been nothing but improvement since then. When this government came into power in 1921 the estimates for the coming year were prepared and, I understand, were largely in excess of the revenue expected. So. if our friends had been returned to power, we would have had a continuation of those deficits which were rolled up in previous years. When hon. members opposite undertake to criticize this government on their financial showing, they do it with very poor justification.
The hon. member went further in speaking of the manufacturers, and said that he for one would be willing to pay his share of any increases in price necessary to keep the manufacturers in business. I suppose the manufacturers will have no objection to accepting money from hon. gentlemen across the way, but I venture to assert that these hon. members and the supporters of the Conservative party throughout the country will be just as willing to accept the benefits accruing from these reductions as will members and supporters of this party. If the hon. member for Fort William wished to contribute something to keep the manufacturers in business I suppose his contribution would be received, but I do not think he was serious in that suggestion.
The hon. member went still further, and said that this country had been treated by the United States as a customer who, having gone in to deal with a storekeeper, had been kicked out of the store. I take exception to that statement; the United States has not treated us in that way. I wish to point out to hon. members who may not fully understand the situation that we in the Maritime provinces are almost wholly dependent upon the United States for a market, and this statement applies especially to the people of Prince Edward Island. We are an agricul-* ural province; we have no industries of any .Jnd, and if this budget works an injury to some other provinces, I certainly do not see that it can possibly be injurious to Prince Edward Island. I do not understand how hon. members opposite representing that province can vote for the amendment, thereby voting against a reduction in the income tax; a reduction in the duty on automobiles; a reduction in postage; against the wiping

out of the stamp tax on cheques and, in fact, against every other item contained in this budget. I do not see how they can do that and square themselves with the people of their province. That is none of my business, however, and I leave it to the hon. gentlemen and their own electors. They are able men, well qualified to judge the situation; they are fair men, and I give them credit for carrying out their convictions as they understand them. So far as I am concerned, I believe that this budget in every particular is beneficial to the people of the province of Prince Edward Island.

Coining to the tariff, I wish first to point out that the difference between the position of the farmer and the position of the manufacturer is very marked indeed; so much so. that there is really no comparison at all. The manufacturer, under protection, can set his own price. He can take the cost of production, add to that the cost of distribution, add insurance, add all taxes on his business, federal, provincial and municipal, including the sales tax, add the duty on the imported article, and to all these he can add a good substantial margin of profit, and then go out and sell his product in a protected market. The farmer, on the other hand, has to sell his product in open competition with the world. There is the comparison between the two, and when our friends across the way talk of protecting the farmer I think they are endeavouring, to say the least, to camouflage the situation. They are endeavouring to pave the way to lining up the farmers of this country in support of a high protective tariff all round, but I think I shall be able to show as I proceed that protection can be of very little use to the farmer when he has a large surplus to export.
Our friends from the Maritime provinces, a great many of them, have been elected on the question of Maritime rights. The provincial papers at that time said that these men were neither Liberal nor Conservative, but that they were supported by a large number of the independent people of the Maritime provinces as Maritime righters, and that they were going to be independent in their viewpoint. But I notice that our friends across the way from the province of Nova Scotia, since coming to this House, have not been very independent in their viewpoint. Whatever their attitude may be in the future, they have up to the present been very strong supporters of the Conservative party, and they have strongly advocated the principle of protection. That, of course, is their own affair. If the principle of protection is satisfactory to the people of Nova Scotia, if protection is essential to that province, our friends are no doubt doing right in supporting that principle, but representing as I do a constituency in the Maritimes which is altogether an agricultural and a fishing constituency, I cannot see how a high protective tariff can be of either direct or indirect benefit to that province or to my own constituency in particular. I do not wish to be considered an
extremist in my tariff views. We realize in the province of Prince Edward Island that if we had free trade with the rest of the world, it would be of advantage to our little province in particular, but none of us has ever advocated that. We are big enough and broadminded enough, I trust, to be willing to contribute our share of any protection that is needed for any legitimate industry in this country, and I think the people of that province, both Liberal and Conservative, will continue to maintain that attitude and be willing to pay their share to see that no industry shall suffer unduly from too radical reductions in the tariff. But we feel very strongly on this point:	Where any industry is receiving
a degree of protection which is out of all proportion to that which it should receive, our people are very, very strong in the contention that that protection should be brought down to a reasonable point which would allow the people of our province to import, if they wished to, these products at a reasonable figure, thereby contributing to the revenues of this country a certain proportion for the upkeep of the government, rather than allowing the whole amount of the protection to be turned into the coffers of the manufacturers. That is the attitude, I believe, of the people of the province of Prince Edward Island.
So far as the automobile industry is concerned, that is only one of the many which we thought was possibly receiving too high a protection, and that a reduction could be made. I have an article here on Maritime rights which appeared in the Canadian Annual Review this year. It was written by W. C. Milner, B.Sc., LL.D., and I should like to put an extract from it on Hansard. The author gives his view of the situation. I am not saying that I accept that view; I simply give it for what it is worth. The writer says that one-half or more of the people of the Maritimes are engaged in agriculture. For lack of markets this industry has practically made no progress in ten or even twenty years.
He goes on to state that there cannot be successful competition against the farmers of Ontario and Quebec in the Toronto and Montreal markets. I wish to emphasize that as a fact which we realize in the province of Prince Edward Island. We cannot compete with the farmers of Ontario and Quebec in their own markets, and it is absolutely impossible ever to think of doing so. The writer goes on to say that the list of articles produced in the Maritime provinces for which there is a demand in the central provinces is exceedingly small. Efforts have been made to extend west the demand for fresh as well

A resolution calling for abolition or diminution of present customs barriers between nations was adopted at the closing session of the inter-parliamentary union here to-day. The resolution, which was introduced by Adolph Braun of the German delegation, calls for the appointment of subcommittee to draw up a plan. It was passed without opposition.

As the hon.
Minister of Finance remarked last week, whatever changes may be made, the budget will continue to be a truly Liberal one' and also very popular.
Now, the question of agricultural imports and exports has been gone into pretty fully by a number of hon. members, but as our friends opposite are featuring it very strongly this session I wish to present a few figures to the House. It is only very recently that our friends of the opposition have been shedding tears of sympathy for our farmers. Although they were in power from 1911 to 1921, during all those years we did not hear very much from them about the needs of our farmers. We all remember the Conservative campaign cry pf 1911: No truck or trade with the Yankees. Well, soon after our friends came into power we find that the largest importation of eggs in our history took place-not all from the United States possibly, but the volume was tremendous. In 1913 we imported no less than 13,158,538 dozen. In 1914 we imported practically a similar amount. Eggs continued to come into this country in large quantities right down to 1921. All through those years our friends were not shedding crocodile tears over the woes of our farmers, in fact they never moved a hand to prevent this gross injustice, as they now term the importation of eggs and dairy produce. I submit it is rather late in the day for the opposition now to try to make the farmers of Canada believe that they are their friends. As has been pointed out time and again, when we have a surplus of products protection cannot be of any benefit to our producers. Take silver fox furs. In my province it is a large item of business and we used to enjoy a splendid trade with the United States. Then the government of that country put on a duty of 50 per cent and shut us out of the American market completely. Will any of my hon. friends opposite say that our silver fox breeders would have been benefited by a retaliatory duty of 50 per cent on similar furs coming from the United States? The proposal would have been absolutely foolish, for it would not increase the price of silver fox furs in the Dominion by a fraction of a cent. The same argument holds good all along the line. We have a poultry association in the island which last season handled about $400,000 worth of eggs. In their report they state that $26,000 worth of those eggs was shipped into the United States, also a large quantity of dressed and live poultry. A duty on these articles would have no effect and would give no benefit to the Maritime provinces in any conceivable way, so the question of the import and export of agricultural products between the countries of the world is one which I really do not think our farmers will take seriously. I am sure that if the tariff board now constituted believe it to be in the interests of the farmers of Canada tQ have protection on certain articles, they will not be slow to recommend it, and I think this government would take that recommendation into consideration. No one is more ready to accept such a recommendation than I, and no one is more ready to see the farmers and fishermen of this country receive some benefit, but until I am shown that that benefit will be derived I do not think it wise to start a tariff war with the United States in which we may perhaps lose some of the benefits we already enjoy.
The question of the Hudson Bay railway is too large to go into at the moment. I was opposed to the construction of this railway until a delegation came to Ottawa last session, and until I saw some photographs showing the work from start to finish; I was then convinced that that road should be completed. I believe both parties are committed to it; I notice that hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House have so expressed themselves, so I do not think it is a party question. The honour of the Dominion is at stake; we should complete this road, for which we are led to believe certain lands were reserved, and some sold, the resulting funds being earmarked for the construction of this railway. If this is the case we should go ahead and complete the ninety-two miles still to be constructed. I must say, however, that as a Maritime man I can never be convinced, that this will be a successful graincarrying route, or that it can be used for the export of cattle, as the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins) suggests. But if there are minerals, fish, timber, lumber and pulp wood in that country we should complete the road and give those people a chance to transport these products. This will help increase the wealth of our Dominion, and I think it is only justice to the people of the west who have been hoping for this road for so long. The photographs which were shown in this building revealed that a work of great magnitude has been constructed at the bay. When we see a steel bridge a mile long extending from the shore to an island to form part of the harbour; when we see the tremendous equipment, the steel bridges built over every stream and river, the grading all done and everything ready for the rails to link up the work at the bay with the rest

The Budget-Mr. MacLean (Prince)
of the road, we should not hesitate one moment. Every member of this House should support the proposition, see that the work goes ahead, then wait for further developments as to the feasibility of carrying grain before further expenditures are made. That is my attitude, and if that route can be made feasible no Canadian will oppose the further development of the port, if it is to be a benefit to the country as a whole.
In dealing with the question of the potato trade of Prince Edward Island there is just one little feature I would like to point out. A couple of years ago the railway management decided to close a small station near my home because of the lack of business; the station had fallen below the margin of business required for a booking station. We took up the matter with the management and pleaded with them to let the station remain open for another year to see what would develop. I wish to put on Hansard what the potato trade of that province will do if given a chance, not only for the farmers of the country but for the Canadian National Railways as well. In 1922 the earnings at that station had fallen below $5,000, and the freight moved was only slightly more than 1,000 tons; in 1923 the earnings were 86.700 and the tonnage about the same; in 1924 the earnings had increased to $9,800 and the tonnage to 2.100 tons, while in the year ending April, 1925, the earnings had increased to $23,370. That is what this country, given a chance, will do for the Canadian National Railways and for the farmers of the province, and I ask this House to do everything possible to assist that industry. The farmers and potato growers there are forced to build their own potato warehouses; it is impossible to ship out the tremendous crop in the fall, so frost-proof warehouses must be constructed at a station, and under the present arrangement the Canadian National Railways will not put in a siding to these warehouses unless they receive full payment for such construction, These sidings cost from $1,000 up, and it will readily be seen that a couple of farmers joining together and building a potato warehouse costing from $5,000 to $8,000 will have a heavy additional expense in building a siding which may cost from 81.000 to $2,000. I would like the Canadian National system to take this matter into consideration and see if some scheme cannot be arranged by which sidings may be built to accommodate these potato shippers. I venture to say that the cars going over every new siding will increase in number from year lo year, and will show a revenue to the rail-

way. If some plan could be worked out whereby a bonus would be given on each car of freight to be applied to pay for siding accommodation, or some similar system for the benefit of the farmers and potato growers, it would not only benefit that particular class, but the country as a whole.
I wish to thank the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) although he is not in his seat, for the splendid assistance he gave in making Prince Edward Island a disease-free area, a statement of the cost of which I would like to put on Hansard. Our products are now shipped to the markets of the world labelled as dairy products from a disease-free area, and I am pleased to be able to state that we are receiving the benefit of this work through an enhanced price for our products. With the permission of the House, I should like to put this table on Hansard. The total cost for covering the whole province was only $57,000 approximately, and the results have been wonderful. The local government have done their share, and I wish to express the appreciation which the farmers of the country feel for tJheir action in endeavouring to put this thing over. The right hon. leader of the opposition is a gentleman for whom I have the highest regard, a gentleman who has the admiration I believe of the people of this whole Dominion no matter what their politics may be, but we find that his party, and he as leader of that party, have not always stood four-square by their policies as they claim to have done. The same inconsistency was shown in their attitude in regard to taking over the Canadian National railway. The right hon. leader of the opposition pushed the resolution through the House guaranteeing principal and interest on the Mackenzie and Mann railway, and to take over this and other roads. But last year, at the time of the election we were led to believe that the Conservative party were willing to abandon these railways and turn them over to private ownership. I do not know whether I am justified in making that statement or not, but that was the information we received in our little province.

speechtext:
That appeared not only in Liberal newspapers, but in the press of Ontario which reported speeches of the right hon. gentleman at the beginning of
the campaign. He went so far as to say that if it was impossible to bring the Canadian National railway system to the position where it would be on a paying basis, something else would have to be done about it. However, I do not wish to take any undue advantage of the right hon. gentleman seeing he is not here. I am glad to see, however, that hon. gentlemen opposite at the present time are willing to own the Canadian National railway system, now that it is making such splendid progress under present management and that they are willing to adopt it as their own creation and stand behind it, I presume, to the limit. I am pleased to see that they have changed their minds, if they did have any intention of abandoning the government railways, and have come to what I believe is the right attitude on this very important question.
Again, in 1923, the policy of the Conservative party as announced by the leader of the opposition was " Ready, aye ready," but in 1925 it was not ready until after a plebiscite or a general election had been held on the question of our participating in overseas wars. So it is always well to remember the old proverb, " People who live in glass houses should not throw stones." I suppose both sides have their faults and that each side cap be called to account for something. If this government is guilty of all the sins that our friends opposite have charged against it, I think our friends opposite need to be reminded occasionally of some of their own shortcomings.
With regard to the interests particularly of the little province from which I come, there are many improvements we need. There is, for instance, a second car ferry steamer. That is something the government will have to consider in the not distant future. The steamei we have now has given splendid satisfaction up to the present, but she cannot go on forever, and our people feel that they should be safeguarded against any return to the former transportation difficulties we had by providing now for another car ferry as soon as possible.
We are always looking for something in the way of branch railways in the province of Prince Edward Island, and I am afraid that we have been waiting perhaps a little more patiently than other parts of the Dominion. I hope our good friends from the west, if the Hudson Bay railway is completed, will not forget that there are other places in this Dominion that should receive some consideration in the matter of branch lines. Particularly is this true of some of the outlying sections of Prince Edward Island which have not
3420	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. MacLean (Prince)
railway facilities to-day. These parts should receive consideration as soon as the management of the railway is able to take this matter up.
In conclusion, there were certain matters referred to by two hon. members of this House at the beginning of this session and speeches made along a certain line which I think should be abandoned. We had the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Doucet) charging the Liberal party with all kinds of practices during the election campaign in the province of Quebec. Then we had members on this side of the House making similar charges against the party opposite. I do not think it is fair to the leaders of both our great political parties in this House to treat them in this way. We have in the leader of the opposition a gentleman of outstanding ability who has given possibly of his best to this Dominion, and I do not think it is right for us to criticize on the floor of this House any attitude he may have taken during the election campaign. On the other hand, I think it is unfair for hon. gentlemen opposite to criticize the leader of this government in connection with these matters. He has given of his very best to this Dominion for the past few years, and I think there are enough really big questions in this country to occupy our time without bringing these matters up. We should leave these personalities alone, and rising above such things, give our public men a fair chance. They are doing the best they can on behalf of this Dominion. Their's is a big task to carry out. Canada is a difficult country to govern, and the members of the administration, it seems to me, occupy a very unenviable position. Let us as members of this House endeavour to see to it in our respective communities that the political leaders, no matter of what party, shall be given that fair play and that considerate treatment which they merit.
In the last campaign flag-waving was unfairly resorted to; it was responsible for the loss of a great many votes to the Liberal party. Let me also say this to Liberal members from Ontario and Progressive members from the west: if there is not as large a representation of these two parties in the House at the present time as there should have been it is due to the fact that we defeated ourselves by running too many candidates. In too many instances there were three cornered fights with Liberal, Progressive, and Conservative candidates in the field. If Liberal and Progressive aims and policies are the same why not stick to our guns and meet our Conservative friends on equal grounds, not with our forces divided. Then, I hope,

we shall emerge from the next conflict with a greater measure of success than rewarded our efforts at the last election-as I feel sure we defeated ourselves in many constituencies, and I trust that the splendid showing made by the present administration in the financial situation of the country will continue, no matter what party may control the situation in the future.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I
join with the last speaker in congratulating our genial friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) on his return to the House.
There is no question but that the budget, which we have been discussing for the past three or four weeks, presents features of considerable interest. Tt will probably be very favourabfy received in the middle west, with perhaps little enthusiasm in Quebec, with some hostility in Ontario, and with very little enthusiasm in the Maritime provinces. The reduction in the income tax was overdue and will be welcomed by all wage earners who are now taxed; but the double taxation on industry which it now introduces is as vicious in principle as it is altogether foreign to Canadian experience. May I point out that respectable people of the middle class who have invested in industry, perhaps the savings of a lifetime, are now to be taxed as a result of their thrift, and faith in Canadian industry. There is no doubt that tax-free victory bonds will, under this budget, command an additional premium.
There is another regrettable feature about the budget. According to the figures presented by the Finance minister (Mr. Robb), the Canadian automobile industry has provided a market for a very considerable quantity of iron and steel to the value, I believe, of $11,000,000. In addition to the reductions of duty already brought into effect I understand the Finance minister contemplates putting this large amount of the material entering into automobile manufacture on the free list. May I say that to the extent that that is done it is going to further unfavourably affect the iron and steel industry which is in a very bad position to-day, particularly in the Maritime provinces, as the minister must be aware.
Coal and steel are the twin industries of Nova Scotia, but the present budget provides no relief and gives no encouragement to these industries. I think that is particularly unfortunate in view of the unfair competition which results from the depreciated currencies of our European competitors, more especially Belgium and Germany. I have no doubt the Finance minister is aware of the fact that during the past winter a considerable ton-

The Budget-Mr. Cantley
nage of Belgian and German wire rods came out to Sydney at a cost of about $9 per ton less than it was possible to produce them at that point. Such a condition of affairs is, to say the least, regrettable. However, I will not labour the point any further.
It is unfortunate that the government took action on the tariff and entirely ignored their announcement in the Speech from 5 p.m. the Throne as to the necessity for careful inquiry by the Tariff Advisory Board before making any changes in the duty. This point has been dwelt on by other speakers, and I will not now further discuss it.
There is another matter which has not as yet been discussed in this House. For the past three or four weeks a committee has been conducting an investigation into the matter of unrestricted reciprocity as understood by a gang of smuggling crooks aided, abetted and protected by officers of the Department of Customs and Excise, with the attendant and consequent debauchery of the preventive branch of the Customs service. May I impress upon both my hon. friends the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs and Excise the absolute impossibility of stopping smuggling in the Maritime provinces and Quebec in view of our enormous coast line, extending as it does from Passamaquoddy bay, New Brunswick, up the bay of Fundy into Minas' basin, thence along the south coast of Nova Scotia, and the entire coast of the island of Cape Breton-which island lies within 150 to 200 miles of St. Pierre, the supply station of the eastern smugglers. Then you have also the entire coast of Prince Edward Island, through the straits of Northumberland, the gulf of St. Lawrence and the north and south shores of the St. Lawrence river and right up to the city of Quebec, a coastline of not less than fifteen hundred miles. On eighty per cent of this entire coastline liquor can be landed and distributed during the entire season of open navigation. I am satisfied that if the Minister of Customs and Excise had at his disposal one hundred armed vessels and one thousand coastguards he would not be able to stop smuggling in that section of the Dominion so long as customs and excise duties remain at their present high figure of $10 per gallon. So long as the duty on a case -of whiskey is $21.50 or approximately one hundred and fifty per cent of the c.i.f. cost and in proportion on other liquors, it is simply impossible to stop smuggling. The c.i.f. cost of ordinary brands of good Scotch whiskey, landed at Halifax or any other port in the Maritime provinces, or in the St.
Lawrence, is about $14. On the other hand the duty is over one hundred and fifty per cent and the spread is so great as to make it impossible for any government to stop this smuggling. The same argument applies to cigarettes. If the Minister of Finance will reduce the imposts to what they were three years ago he will accomplish a dhange for the better. I may be told that hon. gentlemen on this side raised the duties to their present figure. I think they did. And I fancy it was done at the behest of certain "unco guid" people in Toronto and some others of that stripe. When they did so they made the greatest possible mistake in the interests of public morality, sobriety and good conduct in this country. I hope the government will make a change and reduce these duties to at least one-third of those now in force. If they do that they will find that four-fifths of their difficulties in connection with the smuggling of cigarettes, tobacco and liquor will disappear over night, with an accompanying decrease in debauchery, crime and all the evils attending the operations of the nim runner and smuggler.
In regard to the desirability of a national policy for fuel, 'let me say that in no country in the world is fuel a matter of greater importance that it is in Canada. It is the foundation of industry, and without the assurance of a continued supply the capital needed for industry cannot be obtained except on speculative terms. From the heard of the Great Lakes westward there need be no fuel problem, as the British Columbia mines can supply the whole country west of the Rockies and under reasonable, fair and practical freight rates the Alberta .mines can supply the middle west and also can command most of western Ontario. While last year there was a considerable increase in the output of Alberta coal, there was a very decided drop in the production of Nova Scotia coal. Altogether we produced in 1925 slightly over 13,000,000 tons and we bought and brought into this country from various sources, largely from the United States in round figures 17,000,000 tons in addition. In other words we did not produce 45 per cent of our requirements.
The industry in Canada has an investment of from $146,000,000 to $150,000,000 and is entitled to all the consideration possible as regards not only protecting the industry but making this country independent of any foreign country for its indispensable fuel. Unless our policy in this matter is completely changed this Dominion will some day suffer as to both its domestic fuel and fuel for its manufacturing activities. With a national fuel policy providing an adequate duty on
The Budget-Mr. Cantley

the various kinds of coal and fuel, be it bituminous, anthracite or coke, Canada can within ten years be placed in a position entirely independent of any outside source of supply.
Let us consider the situation in the United States. There was a time when we in Nova Scotia despatched each summer from the town where lives the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) more than 1,000 vessels loaded for eastern United States points and an equal number sailed from Cape Breton. The United States government later imposed a duty of SI.75 a ton on our coal and stopped that business instantly with the result that they have developed their own resources; they are to-day shipping into Canada from ten to twelve millions tons of coal annually and they are now by far the greatest coal producers in the world.
Surely we can take a lesson from the experience of other countries. Are we wiser than the combined peoples of all the world? It would seem as though we thought we were, but I am sure and I think most hon. members are also sure that we are not. Every business man, everj' man of any intelligence who reads the newspapers knows what the situation is. The remedy is obvious and I cannot understand why we do not put it into force. Three things we ought to do. We should first impose upon coal a duty sufficient to enable us to control our own market. We should have an adequate protective duty on all classes of coal, coke and patent fuels equal to, say, not less than 25 per cent of the present laid down, e.i.f. cost. That would be, say, $1.25 to $1.50 a ton, the duty to apply to all coal, coke and patent fuel imported irrespective of its origin or the purpose for which it may be used. I have said that the rate should be $1.50 a ton and if it were that duty would be considerably lower than that at one time imposed by the people of the United States on Nova Scotia coal then largely shipped and sold by us to New England cities. Some of my hon. friends may balk at a duty of $1.50 a ton. While the industry is certainly entitled to that amount of protection I wish to emphasize the fact that a rate of duty less than one dollar a ton applied to all classes of fuel will entirely fail of its object, be mischievous and disappointing
I now want to make some reference to my good friend the Minister of National Defence, who is familiar with this subject on which a discussion took place on various public platforms in Pictou county a few years ago when we had the mutual pleasure of
fMr. Cantlev.]
meeting each other during the campaign of November, 1921. My hon. friend at a meeting at Trenton six days before the election made this statement:
After all our discussions about far away politics, the important thing that has to be settled on December 6, is what is to be the future of this town. 'You want to consider between now and then as to which one of the men who come to you and ask your suffrages can best help in changing the conditions as they now exist, and can best bring to the solution of the problems that face you all, that capacity which will mean that once more we will have prosperity where now we have doubt and despair.
Where do we stand in regard to this matter? What is the situation? We have in the candidate of the Conservative parly one story and one story only, from him and his friends:	"We are not going
to make any changes in ithe tariff. You should bow down and worship the National Policy, that second Ten Commandments which cannot be touched or interfered with." That wonderful policy under whose benign sway conditions of unemployment and distress have come which exist in this and other communities? He doesn't propose to change a single line in this wonderful document. Are you going to get much help or comfort from that quarter? Not at all.
He proceeded:
Well, the primary cause of these conditions here is the enormous imposition which has been allowed to be placed upon the carriage of the products of the industries of this country of Pictou. Our coal mines are not working because it costs $2.30 a ton more to carry their coal to Montreal. Your steel works are not working because it costs $4.80 a ton more to send your products to your markets.
My hon. friend was wrong by $1 a ton. It was $3.80, not $4.80. He continued:
T come to you and I say that I speak for myself and my party, and that coming into power, as we will on the 6th of December-
And they did.
-we propose to change those railway conditions, so that you will be able to send your products to central Canada, and thus compete with the Steel Company of Canada, and the Americans ait that point.
He did change them; or his friends did change them; the rates that he then complained of they further increased in 1922 and again in 1924. He continued:
You have been told that there is a wonderful duty on steel. Protection on steel. There is no protection on steel. What is a 10 per cent duty on your products? There must be higher duty put on. I frankly say that I stand for that. I believe in that.

speechtext:
Why did the hon. Minister of National Defence mobilize his entire forces-horse, foot and artillery, commissariat and war chest, and in the dark of the last September moon leave the fastnesses of Pictou, which had supported him for thirty years? Why did he abandon, even as did Kruger, that other celebrated man of war, the wife of his bosom and his little ones, leaving them to the tender mercies of the Tory enemy? Under cover of night he marched from Pictou and dug in in the mountain fastnesses of Antigonish, forty miles away, and to-day he warms his cabin in the vale of Kippoch with peat, the duty on coal being too high. Now he talks about people not having courage to meet him! With whom does the balance of courage lie to-day? I think it is for the minister and not for me to explain any want of courage.
To come now directly to the budget. Iron and steel, the basic industry of civilization, has made but little progress in Canada during the past fifteen years. We have advanced perhaps one and a half per cent in Canada while in the same period the expansion in the United States has been about 75 per cent. During the past year Canada imported about 1181,196,800 worth of iron and steel products, largely from the United States, while the

value of these duty free products imported in 1925 was $15,126,109; in the same year dutiable tonnage was imported to the value of $120,000,000. In 1926 the free tonnage imported was valued at $22,000,000 and the dutiable at $158,000,000.
Here is another arresting fact in connection with the ftiatter. Our free and dutiable iron and steel in 1925 was valued at $134,000,000 or an increase of $46,000,000 over that oi 1924. The point is that the proportions of free or 99 per cent rebate steel is going up year by year, and going up rapidly. We have a tariff that is the laughing stock of any commercial man in any country who has any knowledge of fiscal affairs. Our tariff contains items respecting the iron and steel trade that have not been altered for nearly thirty years. There are to-day in that tariff over seventy items that are either entirely free or enjoy a rebate of 99 per cent, and this country has gone on for years collecting large amounts of duty on certain iron and steel products running into enormous figures only to rebate them again later.
The iron and steel tariff as it now exists is the most irrational and confusedly mixed mass of out-of-date schedules imaginable. Take one item No. 387:
Swedish rolled iron and Swedish rolled stcefl, nail rod3 under half an inch in dameter, for the manufacture of horse shoe nails.
There has been no Swedish rolled iron for use in the manufacture of horse shoe nails imported into this country for years-and still the item remains. Swedish rolled iron nail rods were replaced by mild steel years ago. Then take item 1005:
Steel under one-half inch in diameter or under one-half inch square when used in the manufacture of locks and knobs.
That item was put there when Sir Charles Tupper introduced his first iron and steel tariff in 1887. What does it mean? It means the little spindle that goes through a door lock and engages with the knobs. This steel has been admitted into this country for thirty years free of duty although it could at any time during all those years have been made in any of our mills. Ontario factories have been making locks and knobs for thirty years and have enjoyed ample protection on their product-and still have had that particular item coming in free. I might say the same of thirty other items. Why do we not profit by the wisdom and experience of the United States? There is no such nonsense in their tariff. Take iron and steel. The United States customs authorities have been deal-

The Budget-Mr. Cantley
mg with these matters for sixty years, they have evolved a tariff whose definitions are so clear that they cannot be evaded. Take paragraph 306 of the United States .tariff which deals with steel:
"All 'metal produced from iron or its ores, which is cast and malleable, of whatever description or form, without regard to the percentage of carbon contained therein, whether produced by cementation, or converted, cast, or made from iron or its ores, by the crucible, electric, Bessemer, Olapp-Griffith, pneumatic, Thomas-Gilchrist, basic, Siemens-Martin, or open-hearth process, or by the equivalent of either, or by a combination of two or more of the processes, or their equivalents, or by any fusion or other process which produces from iron or its ores a metal either granular or fibrous in structure, which is cast and malleable, excepting what is known as malleable-iron castings, shall be classed and denominated as steel."
There you have a definition of steel which cannot be got around in any way whatever. Every item of iron or steel that is made in the United States and that falls under any of the categories of iron and steel products is amply protected, with the result that there has been an enormous growth in the volume of these products and to-day that country, in respect to that production, leads the world.
Consider the type of competition which the steel plants of Canada have to contend with. Take the United States Steel Corporation, organized in 1901. To-day it has 138 miscellaneous works and departments, comprising 112 blast furnaces, 34 Bessemer converters, 332 oil heated furnaces, 44 blooming and slab mills, 15 billet and sheet-bar mills, also eight rail mills, seven universal plate mills-I might read the whole list, but I will not weary the House. Consider their resources in another way. They have 237,714 acres of gas and oil territory, 1,407 active gas wells and 246 active oil wells, 20 gas compressing stations, 8 gasoline plants with a pipe line distribution system aggregating 1,285 miles. In 1925 they had a production of 15.738,157,000 cubic feet of natural gas-practically all consumed in their own plants-97,910 barrels of crude oil, and 1,313,088 gallons of gasoline. Look at their ore resources. They have 19 active mines which produced last year 27,996,845 tons of ore, and several other mines in reserve. They have railway equipment, including 1464 steam locomotives, 61,916 train freight card and 2,600 odd other items of railway operating equipment. They have also 139 lake and 35 ocean steamships, and 413 river transport vessels.
Then take their production. The output of the several principal departments for the

Consider what they contributed to the taxation of the United States. Last year they paid in federal taxes nearly $51,000,000, and their volume of business was $1,406,505,195, an increase of about $200,000,000 over the year before, and their total undivided surplus on December 31, 1925, was $521,863,109. That is the corporation and the kind of competition which our iron and steel plants have to meet, and the better to aid them we carry their steel on our canals free of all tolls, and impose a trifling duty-the Minister of Defence says ten per cent-and with what result? Out of seventeen Canadian blast furnaces today we have only six in operation; of open hearth furnaces we have forty odd with about 25 per cent of them in operation.
Consider for instance the situation to-day at Sydney Mines. For the last four years not a wheel has been turned nor a furnace lighted in connection with that plant. There are situated two modern blast furnaces; about one hundred and fifty retort coke ovens; a coal washer, than which there is none better on this continent; five 70-foot open hearth furnaces modem in every respect. This plant is situated on top of the finest metallurgical fuel in the world. Why is it not operated; why have we to-day almost two thousand men, in that town of ten thousand people, without work?
Go to New Glasgow, the home of the iron and steel industry of this country, where all the pioneering work in connection with that industry was done either in New Glasgow or in Ferrona, a few miles away. I left school at less than fifteen years of age, after having a difference with the schoolmaster; he is now in heaven, while I have only reached the House of Commons, which certainly is not thought to be the gate to heaven. I have wrought at nearly everything in connection with the iron and steel trade; I know what it is to get up at six o'clock in the morning; I know what Blue Monday means, and the attractive anticipations of Silver Saturday; I was associated for a period of nearly forty years with the men who were the pioneers.
The Budget-Mr. Cantley

Graham Fraser, Simon A. Fraser, Forrest McKay and Harvey Graham; these were the men whose vision, industry and perseverance fought out in eastern Nova Scotia, long before any steel was made in Ontario, all the problems in connection with the utilization of our own and, later, the Wabana iron ores. 'We built there the first commercial coal washer on this continent; we installed and worked successfully a battery of retort coke ovens, three years before there was a retort coke oven erected anywhere else on this continent. I can claim honestly and with some pride that New Glasgow is entitled to the credit for all the pioneering work in solving the problem of making first acid and later basic open hearth steel successfully from our own and also from the AVabana red hematite ores.
Take the situation at New Glasgow to-day; there you may see a forge and mill plant costing say $10,000,000 or more, and how much work is now being done there? We should have 4,000 men working, as we once had. The situation during the past two years has been such that those men who could not get away, simply because they owned their houses, have had to exist on sixty, seventy and eighty days of work each year. All the young, active men who were not tied down went to the United States, and we have left only the older men who, unfortunately for themselves but luckily for the town, are not able to get away being house and property owners. The Scotia company operating that plant never built a single house for its employees. The men were thrifty, largely of Scotch descent, built and owned their own houses. We have had and have there to-day the most intelligent and capable class of labour, not excelled by any other on this continent, but what kind of treatment are they getting? Absent treatment, under which all the active and energetic young men, the best blood, the best brains and brawn of our country have gone to work in a foreign land. How long are we going to put up with it? Only until the people get another opportunity to give a verdict against the party now posing as the government of this country.
Mr. Speaker, there is a great deal more that I should like to say, but time is moving on, so I will conclude with an appeal to the Minister of Finance, to the government, to hon. members opposite and to all parties in this House to give consideration to a matter which, to my mindi, vitally interests not only the workers of Nova Scotia but the national safety as well. Involved in it are pro-

tection to and extension of the coal, iron and steel industries of this country. The next great world struggle for national extension, development and sea power will be on the Pacific. AA7hen that time of stress and struggle comes-and it may come much sooner than most of us expect-Canada will be involved. I do not suggest that our armed forces will be engaged, but none the less this Dominion will be profoundly affected. One of the combatants will conserve and reserve for their own purpose the basic, indispensable products of coal, oil, iron and steel. In view of such a possibility should not and must not we as a nation now take thought and develop our resources, both as to fuel and iron and steel, the most valuable of all metals, so as to make ourselves entirely independent of any foreign source of supply, and thus comply with the first law of nature, that of self-defence? To that end we must develop our coal resources and stimulate in every way possible the iron and steel industry of Canada; only in that way can we make this Dominion economically independent as concerns all essential materials. Such a policy will bring prosperity and contentment to the Maritime provinces and will be a large factor in the unification, development and safeguarding of the Dominion. I thank you.

The hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean) addressed much of the early part of his remarks to what he called camouflaging the issue by the opposition, and I could not help thinking, Mr. Speaker, that that came with very ill grace from the hon. member. In rising to open his remarks he admitted that he had attempted to camouflage the issue on Friday night in moving the adjournment of the debate, because he expected me to make his speech for him this afternoon. We on this side of the House do not believe in camouflaging the issue; I would not consent to that sort of treatment, and told my hon. friend that he would have to make his own speech. But he had not proceeded very far, Mr. Speaker, before I rather regretted my decision, because I discovered that in large measure he was delivering the speech which I am now supposed to give. Perhaps the House will be the gainer, however, because I will be enabled to delete from my remarks much of the data and statistics which he has already given.
Notwithstanding the fact that I have had the honour and privilege of sitting in this House during the last parliament and up to the present in this parliament, this is the first

The Budget-Mr. Hatfield
occasion upon which I have risen to offer any extended remarks in the discussions which have taken place from time to time. There is a very good reason for that, I think. Hon. members will recall that in the elections of 1921 the province of Nova Scotia, from which I have the honour of a seat, returned to this House a solid contingent supporting the present right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), who was subsequently called upon to form a cabinet. Included in that contingent were such eminent statesmen and parliamentarians as the Right Hon. W. S. Fielding, Hon. A. K. Maclean; he who is now Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald); H. J. Logan, George Kyte, the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Duff), and others that I could mention. Under those conditions it seemed almost superfluous that I, a backbencher, coming to this House for the first time, should be called upon to make any general remarks in the debates as they came before this House, as the interests of our province were so well taken care of by these hon. gentlemen. But you will recall, Mr. Speaker, that something else happened in the province of Nova Scotia since the last parliament dissolved. We had a general election in October last, and the province of Nova Scotia did on that occasion what she has done on many another-she almost completely reversed herself in so far as her party representation in this House is concerned, and today, Sir, we have only three members on this side from the province of Nova Scotia giving support to the government.
The hon. Minister of National Defence, by reason of his departmental duties, can hardly be expected to give the same detailed consideration and time to the debates here as he otherwise might do. The hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg has had his lips effectually sealed by his elevation to the Deputy Speakership. So, Sir, under those conditions it does seem proper and right that I should now rise in my place and attempt to discharge my duty as best I can in presenting to the House the interests of my province as I see them, and particularly of the constituency which I have the honour to represent.
I ask the indulgence of the House. Mr. Speaker, in that I desire to offer the most of my remarks and to plead more particularly with this House on this much vexed and much mooted question of Maritime rights. But before I do that, may I be permitted to offer a few general remarks in connection with the budget itself?
I think there is general agreement in this House and in the country that Canada has at
last, as we say, turned the corner of hard times and is now on the road towards a better era of prosperity and national development. I think, Mr. Speaker, it should be common ground for general satisfaction, and indeed profound gratitude, that that is the case, because we remember, Sir, that when we entered the post-1 war period there were those in this country, perhaps best qualified to judge, who viewed with concern and gravity the position of this country so far as the future was concerned. Indeed, Sir, they went so far as to express grave doubts as to whether or not Canada could ultimately recover and recoup herself from the great losses of that terrible world conflict. It is because the budget statement reveals the condition in this country that it does reveal that I think we should find common ground for general satisfaction and profound gratitude, because there is no gainsaying the fact that while we may not all feel that Canada is all the way on the road to prosperity, she certainly is on the way.
I am not one of those, Mr. Speaker, who think that all this is due to short-time administrations and overnight policies. Depression and prosperity in a country are not as a rule the result of short periods of administration; they are rather the result of long periods of administration and they are not always the result of conditions within the borders oi the country itself. World conditions usually account for prosperity or depression in a country to a greater extent perhaps than the conditions at home; it is international, rather than national. For instance, this country, our Conservative friends say, came through the great world war in as good a condition as or better than any other belligerent country that entered the war when Canada did and stayed in to the finish. I think that is true, and Canada can have a pride in that, but our Conservative friends say: We did it; it is the war-time administration that is responsible for the success of Canada in that war. That may be true, Mr. Speaker but on the other hand, if the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) would permit me to borrow an expression from his spech, it may be also true that our success was in spite of the war-time administration. But I feel that nobody upon reflection will deny that the great contributing cause to the success of Canada in that war was more due to pre-war administrations than to the war-time administration itself. Obviously, Mr. Speaker had Canada been governed by administrations weak and spineless, without courage and vision, the com ditions in the country which we would have had to turn over to the war-time administration would have reflected the character and

The Budget-Mr. Hatfield
quality of the governments that had governed for a decade, a decade and a half or even two decades before, and it is because Canada did possess governments and administrations with courage and vision and the genius to govern that they were able to turn over to that wartime administration a country strong, virile and potent in aid the essentials and in all those things which were vital to withstand the terrible onslaught of that war. Even a government of devils-and I would not suggest for a moment that the war-time administration was a government of devils-could not utterly destroy and wreck our country in the four years of actual warfare. Just so it is true, Mr. Speaker that, a government of angels could not have saved this country from the terrible strain and terrible effects of that awful conflict, and that is why it is, Sir, when we came into the post-war period, that Canada of necessity must have been weakened and broken well-nigh to the point of utter discouragement. That is why it is that when we came into the postwar period, the war-time administration of necessity turned over to the post-war administration a country very much weakened and a country not able to function as she would in peace time. That too, Sir, is why it is that our Canadian statesmen and those who are in the best position to judge did have grave douljts and grave concern in respect to the future of this country.
It is because the budget statement reveals the fact that we have now turned the corner of hard times and that we are now on the road to prosperity, that we must I think find common ground in that situation for great satisfaction and profound gratitude. Our friends opposite, Mr. Speaker, were quite willing apparently to admit that, for the hon. member for South Wellington, who was put up to answer the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) admitted that there was a return of prosperity in this country, but, he said, it was not due to anything this government had done; it was in spite of what it had done; it was all due to Providence, he said. To complete the parallel between the criticism of the present day opposition and the criticism of the old opposition in the Laurier-Fielding days, you will recall, Mr. Speaker, that in the budget revision of 1897 there .were the same dire prophesies made as to what was going to happen to the industries of this country, and when those things did not happen, then was raised the question of the uncertainty; it was claimed that capital would not be invested, and importers would not import, because they did not know what was goinig to happen to the tariff. We have that same criticism to-day- 
tariff instability. Then, when all else failed, and the Finance ministers of those days were able to bring down budgets showing surpluses instead of deficits, they said the government was lucky. It is all there on the records, Mr. Speaker, and it compares almost word for word in many instances with the criticisms of the present day opposition. To complete the parallel, they said that this prosperity had come in spite of the government; it was due to Providence.
I think my hon. friend from South Wellington was hardly orthodox in his treatment of Providence in the remarks he made the other day. The hon. gentleman, it would seem, limited the scope, the power and the beneficence of Providence to certain years and certain times, and to crops rather than to men. For instance, he said that when there was prosperity in 1925 it was the result of good crops; and when there was depression in 1922 and 1923;, because of poor crops, he absolved Providence from all responsibility in the matter. In other words, when there were good crops and good times in 1925 it was a case of thank Providence; but when there were poor crops and depression in 1922 and 1923 it was a case of thank the Mackenzie King government and Robert Forke.

Mr. Speaker, when the
House rose at six o'clock I was attempting to show the similarity of the criticism offered by the present day opposition to that offered by the opposition in the old days of the Laurier-Fielding administration. I had tried to show as best I could that they first talked of the sorrowful wails that were going up in respect to what was going to happen to the industries of Canada. Then they spoke of the uncertainties of the tariff; when better times came they spoke of good luck, and finally the comparison was made complete, I 'thought, when they said it was due not to this government but, in spite of it; and it was all due to Providence.
I had attempted to show that the years 1922 and 1923 were lean years as regards the wheat 'industry of this country. The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) interrupted and advised me that the year 1923 was a good year in the wheat growing indus-'try. But I thought I could recall very vividly the remarks of hon. members representing wheat growing constituencies and I thought the substance of their remarks was that the wheat growing industry was not flourishing in 1922 and 1923. During the dinner hour I took occasion to speak to some hon. members from those western prairies, and they say that while it is true there was a comparatively good yield in 1923 the price was particularly low; that owing to the fact that they had had very lean years prior to 1923 they were not able to overtake their losses; that the wheat growing industry as such was languishing, and that there was no prosperity in the business.
' Our hon. friends opposite should put first things first in their criticism of Providence. They should first thank Providence that this country possesses what she has possessed since confederation and what we hope she always may possess under the guiding hand of an all-wise Providence, namely good administrations. We on this side of the House may be pardoned if we take ocoasion to thank Providence that that great army of wheat growers is represented in this parliament in no inconsiderable numbers, and that they find so much in common between the policies of this government and ihear own that they can give us their general support. We on this side may also be pardoned if we thank Providence that we have the opposition which we possess in this country to-day. May we not be permitted to couple with that a pious 14011-218
hope and wish that that opposition may be maintained for a good many years to come for the general good of Canada as we understand it?
That brings me to the question of Maritime rights. In casting about for some manner in which to give consideration to this subject in order that I may deal with it intelligently, regularly and in order, I have decided to follow the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Smith) who made the first speech in this House for the Maritime righters so-called and who committed them to a general policy. In criticizing my hon. friends I do not wish them to think for one moment that I have any personal suggestions in what I have to say. Thfey are all worthy representatives and Nova Scotia at least has no occasion to feel anything but proud of the men she has sent here to represent her in this parliament. It is their attitude on the question of Maritime rights which I desire to criticize and I will do so as far as possible in a friendly way.
My hon. friend opened his remarks somewhat after this manner. He said: On two main, outstanding, salient points we are of one mind, namely, that we are to give strict adherence to the principles and policies of the Liberal-Conservative party as they have been enunciated in this House and out of it time and again by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), and unswerving loyalty to the leader of the Conservative party in Canada. As regards the last part of that I think there is no difference of opinion between us. It is generally considered that those of the Conservative candidates who would be elected in that election would sit in opposition behind the Conservative leader. But when my hon. friend says that the main, outstanding, salient points which are to govern his attitude and that of his colleagues in this House are that they are to give strict adherence to the principles and policies of the old Conservative party and loyal support to the Conservative leader, I feel I am entitled to take sharp issue with him and to say that as far as I understand the matter that is not the ticket on which they were elected.

They are on record in relation to Maritime rights and I intend to inform this House just what reasons have forced me to the opinion I have formed on this subject. If hon. gentlemen will take up any pre-election issue of the Halifax Herald, the official organ of the Conservative party in the province of Nova Scotia, they will find, in an advertisement covering practically half a page, two very excellent* pictures of the hon. members for Halifax. In the left hand corner there is a complimentary likeness of the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Black) and in the right hand corner an equally good one of the junior member (Mr. Quinn). In the advertisement there is not very much typographical matter, but what there is stands out in bold relief, printed in large black letters. This is what one reads-and bear in mind that this was before the election:
Province above Party. The crisis in its affairs calls all citizens together whatever their party leanings, to act in concert on behalf of their native province. Divided we are destroyed-
May I ask hon. gentlemen opposite whether in their opinion so much of the advertisement as I have just read suggests for a moment that the salient grounds on which members from the Maritime provinces were elected were strict adherence to the old Conservative policy, and an uncompromising pledge of loyal support in this House to the leader of the Conservative party? Let hon. gentlemen turn to another page in the same paper and they will find a larger advertisement carrying, as I interpret it, a general appeal to all candidates in Nova Scotia representing the party opposite. I invite the attention of the House to the terms of this appeal:
Partisan politics has led to the betrayal of the Maritiines.
That, remember, was before the election. But after the election partisan politics evidently is to be the dominant characteristic of hon. gentlemen's attitude towards the question of Maritime rights. To proceed:-
-Partisan politics is dead, dead and dust as far as the people of the Maritime provinces are concerned. As a unit they are going to support the Maritime ticket which is pledged to work en bloc for Maritime interests. Vote as a people, not as a party. Support the Maritime ticket.

fortably seated in this House, take the view that they are here to give strict adherence to the principles and policies of the old Liberal-Conservative party.

My complaint, however, is that they are more Conservative now than they were during the election, for they owe their election to the fact that the great body of independent electors in Nova Scotia took them at their word when they promised to put province above party and subordinate all party interests to the greater demands of the Mari-times. The people assumed that they would support the Maritime platform. But it is one thing to make professions before an election and quite another thing to face the music when responsibility is assumed.
Mr. hon. friend wants to know what, in my opinion. Conservative members from the Maritime provinces should do and what position they should hold. Well, I would expect them, if they wanted to keep faith with their electors, to do as they pro'mised and support the Maritime ticket.
