speechtext:
That will be determined later on; that is just my point, Mr. Speaker. No, I would have thought had my hon. friend played fair with the people who elected him and with this House-because he has _ to come to this House for every bit of legislation that he hopes to get for the benefit of the Maritimcs-I would have supposed he would 14011-2181
have told us something about the history and the origin of this question of Maritime rights, and what the platform was upon which he was elected. Then if he had said what his position was in respect to that platform I would have no fault to find. But neither he nor his friends have referred to it, not in a single instance have they let us know there was a Maritime rights platform. But I would suggest, Sir, that there is a very clear-cut, specific and definite Maritime rights platform. I do not know that it is worth anything; some people suggest it is, others suggest it. is not. But there is such a thing, it is in existence, and the great body of independent electors, yes, and many of the Liberal electors, in the province of Nova Scotia supported my hon. friends opposite because they believed those hon. gentlemen were going to give strict adherence to the principles and policies of the Maritime rights p'atform.
Now, Mr. Speaker. I will try to give you a bit of the history of the origin of the Maritime rights party and the Maritime rights platform as I see it. I may be very far astray, for I ^am speaking as a Liberal from Nova Scotia and I could not be expected to see eye to eye with my hon. friends opposite. But this is what happened as I understand it. In 1920 and 1921 you will recall that we had two elections in that province; in 1920 a provincial election, and in 1921 a federal election. Both of these elections were fought out mainly on the old party lines, and the principles and policies to which my hon. friend now gives allegiance were very much discredited in those elections, so much so in the case of the federal contest that the Conservatives did not succeed in electing a single candidate. In the provincial election they did elect some, but they were hopelessly beaten. Subsequently there loomed on the horizon another provincial election, and my friends got together and said:	"What are
we going to do about it? It is no use to make an appeal on the old Conservative principles and policies, because they are utterly discredited in this province. What will we do?" Well, it is said necessity is the mother of invention. I want to congratulate my hon. friends on the fact that they must possess some person in their party who is endowed in large measure with this inventive genius. He said, "This is what we will do. The census of 1921 reveals the fact that we are the only province in the whole Dominion that is relatively losing population-we a,re the only province in the Dominion that is losing representation in the House of Commons. This all grows out of confederation. Now we will capitalize
The Budget-Mr. Hatfield

the discontent and the unrest that is abroad in our land and we will say that it is all due to the fact that Conservative and Liberal governments alike have utterly disregarded the solemn (pledges of the fathers of confederation in so far as this province is concerned. Repeatedly have we spoken about these pledges, but neither of the old parties has yet brought them to the attention of the federal parliament." And the provincial government, Mr. Speaker, which had been Liberal for nearly forty-three years, was charged with neglect in that they had made no appeal to the federal government to have those wrongs righted. So our Conservative friends in Nova Scotia said, "We will form a new party and call it the Maritime Rights party; we will announce a new platform in which we will incorporate the grievances of this province by reason of the lack of interest taken by the old parties to have those grievances redressed by the federal authorities." Now, that was accepted generally throughout Nova Scotia as a good'thing. It was not a party thing, as I understand it. The Armstrong government in its dying days passed a resolution in which they set forth what they' regarded as the rights of the Maritimes, or the rights of the province of Nova Scotia under confederation. In order that I may not be accused of making up this resolution I will read a copy of it. By the way this does not deal with the Intercolonial railway, it having been treated separately. This is what the resolution says:
Therefore be it resolved that it is the opinion of this House that, subject to section 121 of the aaid British North America Aot, the regulation and control of taxation, trade and the fisheries of this province should be relaxed and modified by the government and parliament of Canada in such a manner that the interest of Nova Scotia may be prejudiced no longer m such matters and that business and industry may be encouraged and stimulated within the province
And be it further resolved that it is also the opinion of this House that the Governor in Council should proceed with the least possible dday to prepare or cause to be prepared a statement of the particulars m which the interests of Nora Scotia have been prejud ced by the economic system of the Dominion ot Canada, and should make application to the government and parliament of Canada for appropriate redress and equitable remedies.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the Maritime rights programme as understood by a certain section of the people of Nova Scotia, namely, that we should come to this parliament and seek to have a modification and relaxation of control of our trade, our taxation and our fisheries, and that there should be an inquiry into the economic system of Canada as it affects the province, and that the status and utility of

the Intercolonial railway should be gone into; these things should all be made the subject of an independent, competent and authoritative commission, or committee or tribunal, or anything you like to call it; that the case of Nova Scotia should be stated before that tribunal, and should then be brought to this House for appropriate redress and equitable remedies. That resolution represents the views of one section of the people of Nova Scotia speaking through its representatives.
What was the attitude of our Conservative friends? Here is the platform, Mr. Speaker, as enunciated by the opposition in that provincial election. I should like hon. members to notice that virtually the same phrasing is used almost in every instance in the enunciation of their platform. This is how it reads:
A competent, independent, honest and authoritative inquiiy into:
(a)	The economic conditions of private and publio business.
(b)	The status and utility of the Intercolonial railway.
(c)	The merits, record and results had, and probably to be had, from the economic system of Canada, their effect upon business interests and prospects of Nova Scotia, including the cost of living and the cost of production.
(d)	Removal of the economic injustices and disabilities under which the province is found to be labouring, and in the event of failure to obtain redress, to submit the question directly ito the people of the province to obtain the will of the electors in regard to the injustices complained of, and in particular to mandate and empower the provincial administration to netition and request the Dominion government to modify or relax its arrangements on the subjects of taxation, trade and fisheries which may be found to prejudice the business and industrial interests of the people and the province of Nova Scotia.
(e)	If after such action the federal authorities will not meet our lair demands with respect to freight rates, trade adjustment and the fisheries, then we must carry our case to the Birtish government for such amendments to the British North America Act as may be necessary to ensure the welfare and existence of the people of this province.
There, Mr. Speaker, I submit is practically the same bill of rights-the same platform- which makes up the Maritime rights platform, the platform which the so-called Maritime rights ticket is pledged to support, namely, that a thorough and competent inquiry should be made into our trade and our fisheries and our taxation, into the economic system of Canada as it affects our province, and into the utility and status of the Intercolonial railway. That, to my knowledge, is the only thing that was ever suggested in connection with this Maritime rights problem as a policy or as a platform until we came to this House and found hon. gentlemen opposite saying they were sent here as Conservatives to support the old Conservative party and its leader.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, another commission. Do my hon. friends repudiate the policies of their own party, when they made that-the very foundation of the whole business? I have here an article taken from the Halifax Herald in respect to this matter of a commission. I was going to come to it a little later, but my hon. friends are impatient and will not wait. I have copies of articles appearing in the Halifax Herald over the signature of Hon. J. F. Cahan, who is now a member of the Rhodes government in Nova Scotia, and who I think, is the only minister of the crown enjoying the unique distinction of having special legislation passed to enable him to become an assistant minister. That was done in the province of Nova Scotia, and Mr. Cahan says:
The candidates who will oppose -the government in the coming election are pledged to obtain: "a thorough and reliable report on the natural resources and assets of the province" and ''a competent, independent and authoritative inquiry into the economic conditions of public and private business, the status and utility of the Intercolonial Railway; the merits, records and results had. and probably to be had, from the economic system of Canada; t-heir effects upon business interest; and prospects of Nova Scotia, including the cost of living and the cost of production."
Everything in connection with Maritime rights establishes that all these issues should be submitted to an independent committee, commission or inquiry, entirely free from partisanship and politics. My hon. friends have very quickly forgotten the position they occupied such a short time ago. They repudiate their own leaders; they repudiate their own platforms and say, " We don't know anything about it, we have forgotten so quickly." You cannot expect much, Mr. Speaker, from a representation in this House composed of men of that description. If my hon. friends will take it good naturedly I have still another evidence which may convince them that this is not a party question. The father of Maritime rights, Mr. W. L. Hall,-[DOT]" Laurie " Hall, as he is called in Nova Scotia-led the Conservative opposition all through the fight, until the going looked good and it was thought that there was a prospect of getting into power. Then a certain gentleman came from Ottawa and usurped the position held by Mr. The Budget-Mr. Hatfield

Hall, taking the throne himself. Both these gentlemen are on record in connection with their independence on this question, and with the permission of the House I would like to read what Mr. Hall said, speaking at Truro. Perhaps the hon. member for that constituency will recall the visit of Mr. Hall, who was on the platform with Mr. Rhodes. This is what he said about the affiliations of the candidates of his party:
It would be hard for him to say what would be the remedy, but if the Conservatives were returned to power they would appoint a commission to investigate-	[DOT]
Then he goes on to say more, and this is tragic:
He is not prepared to say just what fiscal policy is best suited for Nova Scotia, but he was ready to repudiate his stand on protection if, after being in office-
Do not forget that, because it is all conditional on their being in office.
-and ascertaining the needs of the province-
Which he admittedly does not know and will have to geit from this commission.
-he find free trade most beneficial.
Couple with that the declaration of my hon. friends here, who say that the main, outstanding and salient point which should govern our attitude here is strict adherence to the old Conservative policy; I think my hon. friends had better revise their conduct and have a get-together meeting to find out why they are here and what they are supposed to do.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am going to take the plunge which my right hon. leader took when m Nova Scotia, and ask, "What are Maritime rights?" I am going to place myself in the judgment of this House when I say that, after listening to all the hon. gentlemen opposite from Nova Scotia expatiating and expounding on this question since they have been here, I do not believe a single independent member of this House can take pencil and paper and write down a clear-cut, concrete summary of what Maritime rights are. We have heard the hon. members from Cape Breton Island, and I have no fault to find with them. It is perfectly natural; since they do not know why they are here, I can quite understand why they do it. They say this is the whole trouble with the Maritime provinces:	We want a duty on coal and on
steel. Unquestionably that is what their people want them to say; therefore they say it. We come down to Pictou, and the hon. member for that constituency (Mr. Cantley) made a similar statement, and his interests 
are that way. Then we come to the port and county of Halifax, and hon. members representing that constituency say:	No, the
big thing we want is Canadian trade through Canadian ports; that is why the province of Nova Scotia languishes; we have got to have the port of Halifax serve as a sort of sieve through which all through freight must pass. Well, Mr. Speaker, I have yet to be convinced that any policy which does nothing more for a province than to let freight originating in another province and destined , for another place pass through it is basically and fundamentally a sound policy on which you can build up industry in any province. What we must do, in my judgment, is to find policies that will originate freight in the province of Nova Scotia; then we have done something worth while.
There was another hon. gentleman who spoke. Oh, he says, that is not it at all. He was making a very weighty argument, and a good one from his point of view; he was on the question of freight rates, I think. The hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), and a more courteous member we have not in this House;-he never interrupts a speaker except to ask a very pertinent question, and he asks it always in a very gentlemanly way-rose in his place and said: "What would my hon. friend suggest as a remedy?" What was the answer? Unwittingly, I think, the hon. member told the truth. He said: If my hon. friend will induce those who occupy the treasury benches to come over on our side of the House, and let us over on that side, I will advise the government-meaning,
I take it, Mr. Speaker, that the main, outstanding, salient point which is going to guide his conduct in this House is to get into office-like Mr. Hall, down in Nova Scotia, who said: Put us in office, and then we will do these things-notwithstanding that his colleagues had said: No, we are the committee to settle this question and we are going to settle it on the floor of this House, and the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley) said: "We will keep the House in session all night if necessary in order to get the pay for our cow." Yes, Mr. Speaker, it makes all the difference in the world whether you are on this side of the House or on that.
My hon. friend, however, went a little further, and I rather regret that he did. I think he should not have done it; I hope he will not do it again. He rather suggested what we as boys called dirt. He said: "And I will not ask for a portfolio either." He went out of his way to say that; it was not called for at all. Just out of the egotism, I suppose,

The Budget-Mr. Hatfield
that he possesses, he thought: That is the thing to say, and I will say it. But he said more than that. He said: I will be content to advise the government from the very fringes of my party. I want to say to hon. members that if they will take the records of this House and observe from them the conduct of my hon. friend when he had a seat in this House, they will appreciate what he means when he says: I will be content to hang on to the very outskirts of my party if they will only take me back. I regret that the hon. gentleman said that respecting the hon. member for Waterloo.
My hon. friend from Cumberland went further even than that. He said: So far as I know, my leader is the only leader of any political party who/ up to date has given us any tangible and specific remedy for the ills which afflict the Maritime provinces. Well, having expatiated and expounded on the ills of the Maritime provinces as he did, one would almost have thought that he would have taken the House into his confidence and told them what that policy was, but you can read his speech from Genesis to Revelations and you will not find another reference to it. He should at least have done his leader the honour and credit of stating what that policy was. But there is not a word about it. The fact is, his mind and his lips could not work fast enough to denounce the Prime Minister of this country. The Prime Minister came down to Nova Scotia, he said, and asked, what are Maritime rights?-or words to that effect. My observation has always been, Mr. Speaker, that the man who undertakes to bolster up his own case by pulling down his neighbour's has a mighty poor case of his own to bolster up. While I did not have the honour and privilege of listening to the right hon. leader of the opposition when he was in Nova Scotia, I did read the substance of what his remedy is, and I hope no one will repudiate it if I take occasion to recall it.

speechtext:
In effect it was this. He said:	The trouble with Nova Scotia and the
Maritime provinces is that you are denied the markets of central Canada. The fathers of confederation intended that through the operation of the Intercolonial railway you should have those markets, but the freight rates have been made excessive, and you are denied the central markets of 'Canada for your production. My remedy, he says, is that we reduce those freight rates, and whatever loss comes to the railways in consequence the general treasury of Canada will make up.
That sounds pretty good, Mr. Speaker, until you look into it. I took occasion, just as an ordinary business man, not with any particular knowledge of these things-I cannot deal with these highfalutin things, freight rate structures and all the rest of these scientific terms-but as a man who has some production in the province of Nova Scotia for which he wants markets, I can consider this as a business man would have to consider it. So I said to myself:	What are the products for which we
want markets in the central provinces? Which of our products can be successfully marketed, say, in Ontario? Now the production of Nova Scotia runs to about $145,000,000 or $150,000,000 a year. Agriculture accounts for something like $22,000,000 to $25,000,000; coal, about $19,000,000 or $20,000,000; steel products, about $12,000,000; timber, about $12,000,000; and fisheries, about $10,000,000. Now let us take the products of the farm. Does anybody suggest for a moment that the dairy farmer of Nova Scotia can successfully find a market for his butter in Ontario? Why, the very competition he endures in Nova Scotia now is the competition from Ontario butter laid right down on the counters of the stores of Nova Scotia and sold in competition with our own butter. Does anybody suggest that we could successfully find a market for our beef animals or our beef in Ontario? Obviously that cannot 'be done, because the very competition we endure down in Nova Scotia in the beef proposition is Ontario beef. The price we get for our beef in Nova Scotia is what Ontario and western beef costs laid down at the vendors' stores. That is what determines our price. Could we successfully market our fruit, our apples, for instance, in Ontario, where they have millions of barrels for export? Could we find a market in Ontario for our smaller fruits, for strawberries? We ship from my county thousands of bushels of strawberries every year to the United States and go over the tariff, Mr, Speaker, to do it. The hon. member for Argenteuil, speaking the other day on this question of strawberries, said: What we need to do in order that our appetites may not become satiated with American strawberries is to jack up the tariff to a level with that of the United States. Then the hon. gentleman spoke of peaches. He said he was dining at the Chateau Laurier and enjoying a splendid1 dish of peaches until he found out the peaches were canned in the United States. Then, Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. gentleman must have had a nauseating experience of some sort because he retained such a keen recollection Of the incident. Now, I have been interested in the

export of strawberries in my day, and I took occasion to look up the tariff. I went to the Finance department and asked Mr. Russell if he would give me the duties on strawberries and fruits. I have the figures here in his own handwriting and these are the facts:	The
duty on strawberries coming into Canada is two cents a pound. The duty on strawberries going into the United States is one and a quarter cents a pound.

speechtext:
I will answer your question
if you will permit me.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You have made half
a dozen speeches of this kind already. Let me make one. This is my first speech in five years. Does anybody suggest for a moment that through the process of cheapening freight rates we can ever find a market in Ontario say for the timber and lumber we have in the province of Nova Scotia? It cannot be done. What about the products of the mines, the coal mines? Whatever solution you find for the difficulties of the coal mines-heaven knows I hope you will find one; I am depending on the royal commission to find a solution-you will never settle the situation there by the process of Cheapening the freight rates. No government ever did it, and no government ever will do it.
Now as to fish. Gan we, through the process of cheapening the freight rates, ever find a sufficiently large market in central -Canada for our fish so as to enable us to build up a great fish industry in the province of Nova Scotia? Hon. gentlemen must take this fact into account: The man who catches the fish gets from one to two cents a pound for it. Afterwards there is a shrinkage in the fish to the extent, perhaps of forty or fifty per cent. Finally it is sold up here for twenty-five cents a pound, and the -freight amounts to $1.80 per hundred pounds. You can see from these figures where you are going to get in, undertaking to create a big demand for fish in the central provinces through the process of cheapening the freight rates. If we are ever to have a market established here for our fish there must be a lessening of the spread between the price as paid to the producer and wh-at the consumer has to pay for his fish.	-
Will my hon. friends from the Maritime provinces suggest that we could find a good market up here for our live lobsters? Not at all, the thing is ridiculous. And so we might go on through the whole list of our products. There is nothing in the idea. We could not get profitable markets in central Canada for our products even if nearly every dollar of freight Charges was removed.
But there is another side to the question and that is that if you cheapen the freight rate to the central provinces you must also cheapen it on the way back. That will make it more difficult on our part to meet competition; we cannot get away from that fact. If you cheapen the freight rates to Nova Scotia our producers have got to accept lower prices. Let me relate to you a little incident that came to my notice during the election campaign last October. In a pine grove in a strictly rural section of the county of She)-

burne there was a hall dn which we held a meeting, and I noticed that the interior had just been sheathed with pine sheathing. Having been engaged in woodwork in my younger days I had some knowledge of the good milled woods. I saw at once that this wood was well milled and I said to one of the party, "From what mill does that sheathing come?" He replied "We did not buy it here". I asked "Where did you get it?" And what do you think he told me? He said "We bought it in Ontario". Every bit of that pine sheathing was bought in Ontario, the freight to Nova Scotia was paid on it, and it was taken up into that rural district into the very heart of a pine district. There was a stream near on which there were two saw mills, and there was a woodworking plant in the same county. But those mills could not compete with the Ontario product. That kind of thing cheapens the cost of articles produced1 in Nova Scotia, and makes competition that much more difficult for our producers. The "cure all" policy of my hon. friends 9 p.m. opposite will not work. Its effect will be the same as in the case of all Conservative policies as far as the province of Nova Scotia is concerned; that is to say, it is all for central Canada and has nothing in it for the Maritime provinces. That is the way this policy will work.
Perhaps you will permit me to tell you a little story as a relief to the dry details I have been presenting. I do not know whether it is permissible under the rules to tell a story.

speechtext:
It seems, Mr. Speaker, that in a certain home there was an infant which, in spite of the fact that it was given plenty of good nourishing food, wasted away and did not thrive. A specialist was called in who made a careful examination of the infant and then said, "It is a perfect specimen. I cannot for the life of me see why this child does not thrive on the nourishment it is receiving." One day, by accident, the secret of why the infant did not thrive was discovered. The nurse having given the baby its bottle had gone out of the nursery to attend to some other duty. However, she had occasion to return almost immediately and then she made the discovery. It seems that in this home they had a pet monkey which had learned just about what time each day the baby was fed. Accordingly he secreted himself and on this particular day; when the nurse went out he slipped into the cradle,
fij ,	3437
The Budget-Mr. Hatfield
took the nourishment from the bottle, and in order to quiet the crying baby put the end of his tail into the infant's mouth. That is the effect of my hon. friend's policy. Ontario gets the cream and grows fat, and we get the monkey's tail and starve.
My hon. friend said that the Prime Minister came to Nova Scotia in all his ignorance, although he did not use that expression; and he said:	"What are Maritime rights?" It
was my good pleasure to listen to the Prime Minister when he made that speech, and even as politics are played in Nova Scotia our Conservative friends did not play the game. They divorced those words from the whole setting, the whole context of what the Prime Minister said. They singled out that one phrase: "What are Maritime rights?" and they said:	The
Prime Minister is ignorant on that subject.
I never listened to a better speech on Maritime rights than the one which the Prime Minister made on that occasion. He said: "What are these Maritime rights that our Conservative friends down here accuse us of absolutely disregarding? I recall perfectly that the Maritime provinces sent a delegation advertised as being one thousand strong to my government. Before they came to the government they got together and they said: 'We are going to centralize on one great big over-shadowing Maritime right. So great is it that the others are not worth mentioning. We are going to concentrate on that one question and put it up to the government?'" What was it? It was that the Mackenzie King government so frame their policy in regard to the British preference that all British goods coming into Canada would have to enter through Canadian ports direct in order to get the benefit of that preference. The Prime Minister said:	"When you got
to Ottawa you found that through the wisdom of our legislation we had already provided that very thing for you, with the exception of a fraction of one per cent-so much so that you did not make even half a fight in connection with that question." Let me say in passing that this budget proposal takes care of the fraction of one per cent and makes it a statutory measure. The Prime Minister went on to tell us what his conception of the Maritime rights are. This is it and I believe conscientiously and frankly he is basically and fundamentally right. He said, as we say: "I do not think you can depend on the central markets of Canada for your production in this province. What you require is the overseas markets. You must have the markets of the United States, the West Indies,
The Budget-Mr. Hatfield

Australia and the markets of the other dominions."
The other night we listened to a speech by the hon. member for Pictou who portrayed very vividly and correctly the great prosperity which prevailed in Nova Scotia in those old days when we were trading- where? In central Canada? No; we were trading with the nations of the world. My hon. friend said that Nova Scotia ships were to be found on every ocean trade route in the wide world and' he was right. What we need is a return to those conditions. I >am not going to discuss the merits or demerits of the treaties which have been made; that is another argument; but I say that the Prime Minister is fundamentally and basically right when he says as regards Nova Scotia: You will have to get those international markets and your trade must- ibe international.
I am speaking longer than I had intended, but I want to make an illustration of just one commodity that we produce in Nova Scotia in order to show hon. members what can be done if we secure those overseas markets. Let us take the question of fish, about which my hon. friend opposite asked me. If you go to the Marine department under this government and ask the director of fisheries and his assistants what the prospect is for a market for our fish in England, you will be astounded at what they will tell you. They will tell you that the markets of England can easily take care of 1,000 tons of fish a day. We can start that market on 100 tons a day. The market is there ready for us; it is not a market that has to be built up. The fish merchants of England, I am told, will take care of their end of the business; the transportation between Halifax and England will also be taken care of, and what we must have is government assistance at this end- This government must step into the breach and help us in Nova Scotia to build up that great fish industry.
I was going to say that the hardy fisherman has altogether too few friends in this parliament; I am going to revise that and say that I do not believe there is a single member in this House of Commons who is not an absolute friend of the fisherman, but the difficulty is that we apparently have too few members who understand the fisherman's problems and who are in a position to promote his interest in this House. I understand the hon. member for Digby-Annaipolis (Mr. Short) made some reference to the fisherman the other night and made an appeal for him. This is a question on which we should not draw party

lines at all; we should be of one mind in regard to this great industry. But do hon. members know what is required? I am told that if we are to , develop that market we shall have to come to the government and ask for about SI,000,000 covering a period of a few years. If I were to come here and ask this government for $1,000,000 they would have me examined by a specialist, to see what peculiar form of insanity I was suffering from. True, we will spend millions over in the Old Country to bring settlers to Canada in order to settle them on the waste lands of Ontario and the west.

speechtext:
No, I will be brief. There are however, two or three things further which I feel it necessary to touch upon. My hon. friend made some reference to the fiscal policy of the country. Let me say quite frankly that I am not going to make any mere theoretical arguments in respect of the tariff, for I do not attach much importance to that sort of thing. I am not so foolish aa to suppose that under no circumstances whatever can there be any virtue at all in a protective tariff. And by the way, what do we mean by protection? One man who advocates protection himself may be apt to call the other fellow a protectionist also, but surely there is a dividing line. In my view, any tariff levied against imports of goods manufactured in this country is protection even though it be only a tariff of one per cent. It is protection to that extent, at any rate, and if it is 50 per cent, then obviously it is high protection. If you ask me whether I am a protectionist in the sense of affording a reasonable measure of preference, then I say absolutely I am; but if by the question you imply that I should endorse any tariff high enough to shut out all imports, to abolish competition, and to turn the great consuming public over to monopolies and combines, then unhesitatingly I declare I am not a protectionist. As I say, I do not hold the view for a moment that under no circumstances at all is there any virtue in a protective tariff, because when we turn to the country south of us we find a nation who are doing well under high protection. Neither, on the other hand, am I going to argue that there is nothing in free trade to recommend that policy. I do not say that there is no virtue in free trade as it is practiced in England. Indeed, we have only to study the economic history of that country to find that nation has been able to build up the most enormous trade and the most extensive commerce in the world under free trade. Holding these views, I am bound therefore, to conclude that somewhere between the two extremes we must find the remedy, and my conviction is that, in order to arrive at the most satisfactory policy we must take into account all the circumstances and the conditions under which the tariff must function. That is the point I want to make so far as the province of Nova Scotia is concerned. In that province we are so situated geographically that it is impossible for us to prosper under high protection, and in my judgment that is what is mainly responsible for our troubles. Take the automobile industry, for example. You could not establish an industry
The Budget-Mr. Hatfield

for the manufacture of automobiles in the Maritime provinces; you would be obliged to come to upper Canada, the centre of distribution and population. Competition alone would force you to select that field. Nor could we supply the market created by the new industry in Ontario with our production under competition. But, under present conditions, when we buy an automobile we are compelled to pay the tariff and all surcharges, and that is the tragedy of our situation in Nova Scotia. We have to buy from a highly protected market everything we require, and sell in competition with the wide world. The province of Nova Scotia simply cannot exist under such conditions.
My hon. friend referred to the royal commission on Maritime rights. I cannot for the life of me understand why it is that hon. gentlemen opposite do not hail the appointment of a royal commission as a great Maritime victory, to use the Halifax Herald's description. It is undoubtedly a great victory for the Maritime provinces. There has never at any time been an organization of any kind in the Maritime provinces that considered the question of Maritime rights on a wide scale, that did not preface everything it had to say with the opinion that an investigation must be made, and by an authoritative commission independent of party politics. And that is the basis of a proper investigation. My hon. friends' associates in Nova Scotia are not averse to commissions. What did Premier Rhodes do? Speaking as a Liberal I am going to concede a good deal and admit that he did a very wise thing when he went overseas and got Sir Andrew Duncan to come and investigate the coal strike. Sir Andrew was well received in the province of Nova Scotia, and his report was given careful consideration, and this because the public knew that he was not tied by political strings but was entirely free to investigate the matter as he thought fit. They therefore accepted his verdict. I say, therefore, that it is an earnest of good faith on the part of this government that they should select Sir Andrew Duncan as head of the commission to inquire into the Maritime situation from the national standpoint. Hon. gentlemen say that they want this to be an inquiry of the House of Commons; they want members of parliament on the investigation. Let me tell the House that the Rhodes government appointed a committee of members of the local legislature to inquire into certain questions affecting the agricultural industry in that province. These gentlemen came to my county and held an inquiry into agriculture there and the people pleaded with them to do something to put

our district under the restricted area, having it declared free from bovine tuberculosis. When the commission reported back they treated this request with silent contempt; it is not even mentioned in their report. I am told that what they did recommend in substitution was that every one of the farmers of Yarmouth and surrounding districts should keep a colt! That is the solution they offered the farmers there jfor their difficulties in connection with their troubles. The farmers in western Nova Scotia know very well that it costs twice as much to raise a colt to salable age as can be procured for it when sold, and that if they followed the advice of the commission, instead of making two blades of grass grow where one grew before they would simply be pulling up the one already there and leaving only a hole in the ground.
Now, is there anything in this budget that hon. members from Nova Scotia can vote against? Can they vote against the abolition of stamps on receipts, against the reduction of the sales tax, against the reduction of the income tax, against penny postage? Above all, can they vote against the provision in connection with the British preference with regard to the entry of goods into Canada from the United Kingdom direct through Canadian ocean or river ports? Can they do it, Mr. Speaker? If I would not be misunderstood, I should like to ask:	Dare
they do it? What will they do with the reduction of the duty on automobiles? We know what they did in the last parliament; almost to a man they stood up and voted for it. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Black), who represented the Conservative party of Nova Scotia in that parliament, went out of his way to state his position. He said this, Mr. Speaker, and, mark you, the tariff on automobiles was not under discussion at that time. As I say, he went out of his way to make this statement:
I protest just now against the protection given to automobiles. It is beyond all reason that you can go across the line and (buy a machine for half what it costs when you have to buy it in Canada. That protection is not what it should be.
What is he going to do in this parliament with respect to this matter? I am told that some hon. gentlemen opposite made a canvass in their campaign and said-I cannot vouch for this-* that that was what they believed in and what they were going to support. If there is any single issue our hon. friends will be watched on-and I do not want to intimidate them-it is as to what they are going to do in regard to the reduction of the tariff on automobiles.

The Budget-Mr. Tolmie
Now, my hon. friend mentioned confederation. I do not intend, Mr. Speaker, to go into the history of confederation as respects Nova Scotia. Every hon. gentleman knows that we did not go into confederation voluntarily. We were not permitted to give an opinion on the question. Mr. Fielding said in this House in my hearing that we were booted and kicked and sold into confedera-. tion. Sir, we were not sold, because a sale always involves a consideration, and we received no consideration. WTe were simply given into confederation. But what happened then? The best thinking people of the province, once we had become a part of the Dominion, said, "We will undertake to build up a sound, sturdy Canadian sentiment in the province, we will try to make our people Canadian." And so they put it in their literature and taught it in their schools and then-press, and they succeeded. But just the same there is another sentiment in Nova Scotia. They are not satisfied with the way in which they came into confederation, they are not satisfied with the relative progress, I was going to say, but rather, lack of progress, which has taken place since. So there has grown up quite parallel with the one sentiment that other sentiment of unrest and discontent; and if a certain resolution moved in the local legislature a few years ago looking towards secession had been allowed to get its head above water, my conviction is that we would have been astounded at the result of the referendum which was proposed in that resolution. Not that I suggest for a moment, Mr. Speaker, that that would have been the sane, serious, sober, considered opinion of our people; I think it would not have been that; but, with the unrest down there and the propaganda that would have been used, our people would have been swept off their feet on this issue, and that is why that resolution was not allowed to be proceeded with.
But, Mr. Speaker, this question of confederation is one which I am sure, every hon member in this House and every hon. member in the Maritime provinces should take very seriously. Our people will never support secession unless every last resort has been exhausted. But should they do so it will not be with gladness; it will be with sorrow and very grave regret after every possible avenue of escape from such a grave step has been sought. But, Mr. Speaker, if the public men of Nova Scotia continue to play party politics with this grave issue, then the great union which forms confederation will always be threatened and in doubt. If the interests of the province are to be sacrificed upon the altars of political partisanship, then confederation can not and will not endure and, I go so far as to say, confederation should not endure. But if our public men will rise above their party prejudices and their party passions, and will earnestly seek for the light, I am sure a way will be found. When the province of Nova Scotia can march shoulder to shoulder and step to step-with the sister provinces on the road of national prosperity and national development which we all hope for, then and only then can we strike the word "secession" for all time from our vocabulary so far as Nova Scotia is concerned.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it had not been my intention to say anything on the budget, having spoken at some length on the Address a few weeks ago. However, there are one or two points which I desire to bring to the attention of the House, and on looking over the resolutions which will come before us in committee a little later on I find I shall have no opportunity there to express myself, so I am compelled to take advantage of this occasion.
I was very much interested in the eloquent-address of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Hatfield). He stated that it was his first speech in five years. He certainly has done very well indeed. I was rather struck, however, by his remark that Nova Scotians were nurtured in their youth by sucking a monkey's tail. I glanced around the House and the first man I caught sight of was the Deputy Speaker, then I noticed the fine looking specimens from Nova Scotia on the government side, and also the equally fine specimens on our side, and I came to the conclusion that it must be a pretty good monkey.
The hon. gentleman's statement with regard to what was said during the election by the hon. gentlemen from his province who now occupy seats on this side of the House interested me too, because apparently what they had to say on that occasion was very successful indeed and was accepted by the people of Nova Scotia. So far, then, as to following the platform of our right hon. chief, I would say that he has declared himself quite clearly for Maritime rights, and therefore hon. gentlemen from the Maritrmes on this side of the House have every reason to follow the present leader of the Conservative party with the fullest possible confidence that he will give to Nova Scotia and other Maritime provinces their rights when opportunity offers.
I was astonished by one statement made by the hon. gentleman to the effect that the
The Budget-Mr. Tolmie

solution of Maritime rights lay in the hands of the Liberal party. For a moment I was .staggered, because I was wondering what the Liberal party in Nova Sootia had been doing for the last forty-two years, and I thought that if they do not do any better in the next forty-two years all of us will have passed away and it will not matter very much.
Now, with regard to the budget, the government in preparing it has ridden absolutely true to form as far as keeping its promises is concerned. In 1919 at their great convention held in this city the Liberal party made promises which they failed to carry out when they obtained power. Then again on the hustings during the last election and on many occasions since, finally in the Speech from the Throne, the government made a clean-cut declaration to the effect that nothing drastic would be done with the tariff until the tariff board had given each specific case careful consideration and reported to the government. As hon. gentlemen are all aware, after making that clean-cut declaration in the Speech -from the Throne a tariff 'board was appointed in April, three or four months later, and eight days afterwards the government brought down the budget in which they took a directly opposite stand. Everyone knows that the Speech from the Throne is looked upon by the people of this country as being important; they consider that it carefully and thoughtfully outlines the policy of the government for the session, and in addition they make every effort to be present to hear this important declaration read. There is a fight for seats in the Senate, and you will notice that many members of the House of Commons appear here in their best bib and tucker, wearing their Sunday suits and with their hair done up a little differently from the day before. I remember a few years ago one man- thought this such an important occasion that he appeared here in the middle of the afternoon arrayed in all the glory of full evening dress, and made a tremendous impression. That is just an indication of how important the Speech from the Throne is. But now we find that it has been entirely forgotten by this government; they have cast it aside, utterly ignoring the tariff board which they appointed, and taken a directly opposite course. So long as this government is in office we will find that there will not be very much importance attached to the Speech from the Throne, and it will become no more noticeable than the announcement of a new guessing contest appearing in our daily papers. After all, under present conditions, it is nothing more or less than a guessing contest.


Another extraordinary statement was that the government had given the matter of the tariff on automobiles very careful consideration for a whole year. It is very remarkable that if they studied this for a whole year, in the month of January, after taking advice it is to be presumed from experts, they arrived at one conclusion, and in the month of April they completely changed around and came to another. The general understanding was that they had taken some advice, but they took it from the third group in this House, and it was offered in such a way that they could not refuse to listen. These conditions have a very serious aspect because that sort of thing breaks down the stability of business; there is an uncertainty prevailing among our business men; capital is afraid to invest here under these conditions because it is not known what sudden change is going to occur while this government is in office.
Some hon. members have tried to make us believe that the farmers of the United States, after giving careful consideration to the matter of the tariff, have come to the conclusion that they do not want any more protection. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar), speaking on April 22, made the following statement:
I find now that the farmer bloc in the United States have turned against the high tariff and they are crying out against it. I believe they are appealing to congress to make a change.
Let us look into that statement for a moment to see if that is really the case. In connection with dairy produce we find that just a short time ago, when the large quantity of butter which had been held up in Australia and New Zealand through a seamen's strike was released and attempting to find a market all over the world, some of it was shipped into the United States. They promptly responded by placing a tariff of some twelve cents per pound against it, increasing their tariff from eight to twelve cents. That is just twelve times as much as our government think necessary in order to protect Canadian dairymen against the same butter, or three times as much as they think necessary to protect our farmers against American butter. In looking over the situation we find that practically everything the American farmer produces is under protection and that many of the articles he commonly purchases are absolutely free, with no tariff whatever.
There is one commodity, however, which has not been given protection; I am now referring to hides. We find that, when the Fordney tariff was introduced-and I may

The Budget-Mr. Tolmie
say that the farmers took a very prominent part in putting that tariff through-some of the leading agriculturists objected to the tariff on hides because they thought it would raise the price of shoes. They did not realize that the price of hides has very little to do with the price of the finished product. It was also stated that the American, fanner complains that the tariff affords the dealers an opportunity to fix prices. We find that many of the articles on which prices are fixed in the United States have no tariff whatever. I might mention gasoline, and many agricultural implements which are sold . in zones according to the location of the market. If it is in Montana or the central western states there is a certain price set by the implement dealers at which the implements are sold, and on many of these articles there is no protection whatever. In the matter of rough lumber prices are fixed by the dealers and there is no tariff, while the same thing applies to shoes.
We find that after all the cost of distribution has more to do with the final price than has the tariff. According to the United States Department of Labour, out of every dollar's worth of bread sold in the United States-I am speaking now of wheat bread, and there is a protective tariff of 42 cents per bushel on wheat-the farmer gets 16.8 cents; the transportation companies get 4.4 cents; the elevator companies 0.8 cents; the miller 6.1 cents; the baker 57.4 cents and the retailer 14.5 cents. Accordingly it will be seen that the baker receives nearly four times as much as the farmer, the retailer gets almost as much as the fanner, and those two together receive 71.9 cents, or nearly three quarters of every dollar. It will therefore be plain that the cost of distribution is one of the reasons for the fixing of prices, and we find that there has been a tremendous increase in that cost. Rents are higher; taxes of all kinds have increased, and wages are very much higher also.
Now let us see whether the United States really wants a lower tariff. I mentioned the matter of butter a few moments ago, and I may say that the dairying interest of the United States is perhaps one of the largest branches of agriculture, owning 25,000.000 milch cows valued at $1,287,000,000. Then look at another section of the cattle business, that of beef cattle breeding, and see what they think of the tariff. On December 11, 1925, the annual convention of the California Cattlemen's Association was held in San Francisco, and a resolution was passed requesting congress to pass a bill imposing an
import duty of 6 cents per pound on green hides and 15 cents per pound on dry hides. In the same month the Nevada Land and Live Stock Association held its annual meeting at Reno, when a resolution was passed favouring a tariff on hides and non-edible fats, two by-products of the packing house. Then the Texas and Southwestern Cattle Raisers' Association held its annual meeting at Fort Worth and passed a resolution demanding the imposition of an import duty of 6 cents per pound on green hides and 15 cents per pound on dry hides. To give you an idea, Mr. Speaker, of what that proposed tariff really means, let me say that green hides were selling in Calgary last week for 5 and 5| cents a pound.
The New Mexico Cattle and Horse Growers' Association, at their meeting held on March 15 and 16 last, at Albuquerque, passed a resolution demanding an adequate duty on the importation of bides and canned meats. The Colorado Stock Men's Association, at their meeting held on June 13 of last year, emphasized that a tariff on hides was necessary, and made a protest against the continued purchase of foreign meats for the army and navy. I have here also a resolution passed by the Colorado Republican Association, asking for the same tiling.
Here is a portion of a letter I shall quote to you, appearing in the Producer, the official organ of the American National Live Stock Association, published in Denver. This correspondent says:
Nothing is realty the matter with the hide market at this moment but the fact that the United States, by reason of free trade, is a dumping ground for the surplus hides and skins of (the wide, wide world. The Can.ad an pucker peels a hide from a steer, and sends it to this market free, that would have been taxed two cents n pound had it entered on the animal's bark. During the nine-month period ending with September we imported hides and skins to the value of $77,581,000, compared with $54,551,000 during the corresponding period last year, which is one reason why the market collapsed.
A reduced take-off may improve the situation, but, with South America, Australasia, Africa, and Asia dumping hides into this market, the prospect is anything but luminous. Consumers are paying war prices for footgear, and the shoe industry is bragging about prosperity. But for the fact that hides are a byproduct of. the cattle industry, the present situation would be intolerable. It is in striking contrast to the stout prop inserted under the sheep market by rising pelt prices.
These beef men that I have been quoting from have about forty million head of cattle under their control in the United States, valued at $1,052,000,000, indicating that they are a very important factor in the agriculture of that country.
The Budget-Mr. Tolmie

No protests are received from the sheep men. They are enjoying great prosperity to the south of the line at the present time, and this was brought about toy very heavy tariffs ranging from 50 to 100 per cent on wool. In addition to that, shortly after the war, when Australia and the Argentine were shipping lamb and mutton carcasses into San Francisco on the one side and into Atlantic ports on the other, the American people took hold of the matter promptly-they did not put off or argue about it or ask the advice of any third party; they promptly put on a tariff to keep out that mutton and lamb, and the sheep industry in that country is in consequence in a very fine condition to-day.
This matter of hides has an interest to the Canadian people. It shows the absolute folly of leaving a market wide open to be dumped into by all parts of the world. Just imagine $77,000,000 worth of hides being dumped into that country when these people already possess 65,000,000 or 70,000,000 head of cattle.
There is one other factor by which we can judge farming conditions on both sides of the line. With these two countries lying alongside each other, both speaking the same language, and living under practically the same conditions, we shall always find a certain amount of travel from one side to the other. If times are better in the United States, then our people will flock over there and settle on the land or go into business there. If times are b'etter on the Canadian side, then we find our American friends coming north to locate on this side of the line. What have been the figures during the last four years regarding our immigration and emigration across the line ? During the four years ending 1925, 46,218 more people left Canada and crossed the line than arrived from the United States and settled in this country, indicating that our people were going to the country wuth the high tariffs, where things were protected, where the markets of the farmers were protected and taken care of by the government on that side of the line, as against wide open markets and low tariffs in this country, where we have to compete with Chinese, Japanese and low wage countries all over the world.
You will see by the figures that I have given that the American farmer, instead of wanting his tariff lowered or removed altogether as has been indicated by some of the speakers in this debate, is clamouring for an even higher tariff on many of the products of the farm.

There is one other point, Mr. Speaker, that has interested me in this debate. I have been rather surprised to hear the home market sneered at in some parts of this House. Let us take a brief glance at our market situation. In Canada we have large areas of agricultural land, but we find that we cannot consume all that we produce here. We must find an export market for our surplus products. We have two opportunities on a large scale that are open to us, the one market lying to the south of the line in the United States and the other across the water in Great Britain. We find that the market to the south of us, the most convenient market, the one most easily and cheaply reached, is barred to us to a very great extent owing to the high tariffs prevailing in that country since 1922. We find, on the other hand, that to ship to the Mother Country necessitates in some cases, from such points as Calgary, for instance, the shipment of our live stock and other products many thousands of miles by land and many more thousands of miles by water before they reach that market in Great Britain. We must realize, too, at the very inception that this cost of transportation to market is charged in the sale of the product; that is, a deduction i3 made when the product is first purchased to cover that cost. Anyone would imagine that under those conditions in this country of large distances, with a sparse population, with more railroads than we can properly maintain at present, and with other costs existing in this country, our people would value at once the importance of developing a home market here which would give us the opportunity to sell many of our products within our own country without going to the cost of paying very 'heavy freight rates on our products to outside markets. Canada in my opinion is not going to thrive to the greatest extent by developing agriculture alone, although I have been connected with 'agriculture all my life and am a farmet yet. Canada is not going to thrive by the development of industry and manufacturing alone. But when we get these two working in combination, we have the one creating a very important market for the other, and in that way we can bring about a prosperity in this country that has never prevailed here before. I think the most fortunate farmer is the man who can look out of his window and see five or six smoke stacks in active operation within easy distance of his farm, guaranteeing to him a ready market night at hand for all of his products. Under those conditions he saves all

The Budget-Mr. Tolmie
the extra freight that the man has to pay who finds it necessary to export his goods to market.
In the exportation of our surplus products there are three or four things to which we have to give careful attention if we are going to meet the competition in other lands. One is to see that we furnish in these markets our product in such a way as these markets demand. We must see that the quality is first-class in every respect. We must take care that the products are always of a uniform quality, being the same to-day as to-morrow and a year from now. Another point we must take care of is to see that we ship in sufficient quantities to meet the demands of the market, so as to maintain the sale of our products there, and be able to fill any further demand that the market may require from time to time.
The other day I was struck with a statement that was made here about the sale of our steers across the line. One hon. gentleman stated that we must have access to the United States if we were to get rid of a certain quantity of our cattle, because they were not acceptable in the British market. I admit that a large number of our cattle would sell better in the United States than in Great Britain, but there is one thing that we must not lose sight of, and that is that the farmers of the United States took a very active part in putting this Fordney tariff into effect and in placing this duty on live stock and other products, and they are going to keep those duties there just so long as they think they are going to benefit the American farmer. They are not going to lower the duty as the result of any appeals we may make to them. We would have to show them that they could make more money by lowering the tariff than by maintaining the present duty. These cheaper steers being barred from the United States-and they are not acceptable in the Old Country-the problem remains very largely in the hands of the Canadian farmer himself. His object then must be to improve the quality of these steers, first, by better breeding and then by better feeding. I want to emphasize the necessity for better feeding, for the reason that it matters not how well you breed a steer, if you starve him during his growing years you will find that you have only got a scrub steer. By good breeding and good feeding you can furnish a steer that will meet the market requirements in any part of the world. Let me point out too that the farmer is suffering a very heavy loss by producing animals of scrub quality and starving them in addition. In the first
place he loses when it comes to marketing his cattle. During the months of September, October and November a large number of cattle are sent to market and their value will run from a cent and a half a pound to six and seven and even eight cents for animals of first-class quality at that time. In the first place the farmer loses in price on account of the poor quality of his stock, and in the second place he suffers an additional loss by reason of lack of weight, a result of having starved the animal.
There is one other point I should like particularly to refer to. I wish to endorse what the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie) had to say with regard to the manufacture of our raw products at home as far as possible. We all realize that this cannot be done in a day. We all appreciate the fact that a good many of our raw products will have to find an outlet in other markets for many years -to come; but we can begin and manufacture as many of these products at home as we possibly can. Keep your dollar at home and get another chance at it is a very excellent slogan .to follow. A dollar sent out of the country is gone forever, but spend a dollar with your neighbour across the street and you find that you will get that dollar back after a while. I was much impressed during the early Klondike days when Seattle was making a very strong effort to get much of the trade in the Yukon country. If a man went in there to outfit they never let go of him. If the store he went into could not furnish him with the goods he needed they phoned over to their rival across the street so that, 'he could supply whatever was necessary. In that way they kept their dollars in Seattle, and Seattle to-day is one of the largest and most prosperous cities on the Pacific coast.
There is one other matter I wish to refer to, and that is the matter of cement. We have on the Pacific coast two large cement factories near the city of Victoria. One is located at Tod Inlet and the other at Bamberton. These plants, which are about two miles apart, are located .about fifteen or seventeen miles northwest of the city of Victoria. Both were built up by Canadian and British capital; they are entirely British in their capital. They represent a total investment of about $3,500,000. The plant at Tod Inlet has been closed for a period of five years because they could not find a market for its product. The plant at Bamberton is running about three-quarters time, grinding up six hundred tons a day of lime rock and shale and manufacturing this into cement. Last year this

The Budget-Mr. Tolmie

one factory spent $600,000 on wages and materials required in the process of manufacture, as well as in meeting taxation.
Now I wish to outline very briefly the process of the manufacture of cement so as to make my point clear when I reach it in a moment or two. These two kinds of rock, shale and limestone, are first blasted out of the bluff and the ground three times under what is known as the wet process. It is ground down until it is practically as fine as flour. It is now known as slurry. Then this material in its wet condition is put into large tanks. It there undergoes a thorough mixing and three or four per cent of gypsum is added for the purpose of preventing the cement from setting too soon when it is put into place. This mixing process is very thorough indeed. At this particular point the chemists make an analysis of the mixture in order to see that it is uniform in every possible respect. Then this material is pumped into long kilns that revolve very slowly, these kilns being about one hundred and eighty-five feet long and nine feet in diameter. The slurry goes in at one end of the kiln, which is slightly tilted. At the other end finely powdered coal is used as a fuel for firing, and a temperature of 2,700 degrees Fahrenheit is developed. The slurry passes down through the kiln and when it reaches the heated area the moisture is given off. When it is exposed for a period of about three hours to this high temperature it assumes what is known as the clinker stage.
That represents seventy-five per 10 p.m. cent of the process of manufacturing. All that is necessary afterwards is to grind the material into powder, and sack it. What we are dealing with just now is the fact that this material is being shipped from Japan in Japanese ships at a ballast rate which is merely nominal. It crosses the Pacific and comes into competition with the cement produced on this side. To give you an idea of what the competition is like let me say that the machinery required in the manufacture of cement in British Columbia is very expensive; heavy taxation federal and provincial, has also to be met. As to labour, white men are paid from $4 to $6 a day for a day of eight hours. The price paid for Japanese labour in cement factories in Japan averages only 98 cents per day and the workmen work from ten to twelve hours. The cost of production in Japan, therefore, is only a very small portion of the costs of the manufacture of this material in Canada, f Mr. Tolmie.] '
Now, there is no chance for any of our humourists in the House to indulge in any of the old, stale jokes with respect to infant industries. This industry is not an infant industry at all. However, I wish to approach the consideration of this question from the broad principles that we want Canada to be a country in which we can pay decent wages, and where we can maintain a fairly high standard of living for our working people. One of the greatest attractions which this Dominion of ours presents is the fact that a man can come here, can work for reasonable wages, and if he is thrifty and will take care of his earnings-if he is a Scotchman there is no possibility that he will fail in that particular respect-he can very soon improve his conditions and surroundings, and by the time he has reached middle age or a little over he will be able to retire in comparative comfort. That is one of the attractions of Canada, and if we can only continue that attraction by maintaining a proper standard of living for our working people and paying them decent wages we shall not only be able to retain our own people but also attract desirable immigrants from outside. I do not want for a moment to hold up the idea that Canada should be known as a cheap country. I never saw a cheap mining camp that was any good; when it got to be a cheap community everybody left it. Neither have I ever known a cheap country that amounted to very much. If there are any persons in Canada who want to live in a cheap country let them cross to the other side of the Pacific where they can be accommodated at any point. We want to maintain Canada as a decent living country, where decent wages will be paid, where we shall have a reasonable standard of living and where we shall not experience oriental competition. The desirability of the last-named condition was recognized long ago in British Columbia where we have gone to the extent of passing certain legislation in order to exclude oriental competition from Canada. If that has been necessary in the case of orientals themselves, is it not more necessary to keep out the cheap products of oriental countries when they are brought into competition with the products of our own country? Why should we pay for the building up of homes in Japan? Would it not be far better to help Canada by building homes in our own country and furthering its development by having our natural products manufactured by our own people? Is there anything more ridiculous than the spectacle of a ship entering the ports of British Columbia

The Budget-Mr. Euler
with manufactured rocks when there are three huge ranges of mountains extending from the far north to the American boundary containing enough shale and limestone to supply this whole continent with cement if it were necessary? Our inability to meet the situation is certainly no reflection on our workmen or on the people who own those industries in that part of the country. The matter is simply one of low standards of living and low wages, as I have tried to make clear in my previous outline of the subject. These are the things which make it possible for those countries to place their goods on our market at such a price that we cannot compete.
Just in closing I should like to call the attention of (the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) to this particular situation and ask him to take such steps as are necessary to protect our working people and those who have money invested in this industry on this side to such an extent as to enable us to hold our own in this market. If necesary I would ask him to invoke the dumping clause if an opportunity is found of doing so.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
the best authority in Canada, that $100,000,000 could be saved by a combination of the two railway systems. The hon. member for South York a few weeks ago raised that to the huge sum of $200,000,000, and last week he increased it to $300,000,000. I desire to dissociate myself from any such hopeful prediction as that. Indeed, I do not press the question at all at this time. The railways have been very prosperous in the last year, and for that reason some of their difficulties have been removed and the question is not a live one. I can however conceive of a situation when conditions may not be so good as last year when this may become a live issue. I think I am expressing the wish of the great majority of the Canadian people when I say that whenever and if an amalgamation comes about, it will be under public and not private ownership. If the discussion we had last year had no other effect, it did at least something to destroy the propaganda which was so active and which looked to the amalgamation of the National railways with the Canadian Pacific under the control of a private corporation.
I should like to make reference to a report issued by a committee of the upper house-a report to which no attention whatever has been paid, and quite rightly so. I am referring now to a report of a committee appointed by the Senate last year to investigate the railway situation. That committee made a superficial investigation in camera and issued a report in which various methods of dealing with the situation were outlined. One method was favoured above others, and it was to the effect that the two great railway systems should be combined under one management; that the shareholders and bondholders of the Canadian Pacific should be guaranteed a fixed dividend in perpetuity, and that after all other obligations had been met, the resulting profit, which must be very great, should be divided equally between the security holders of the Canadian Pacific and the government of Canada. I was not surprised that the people of Canada paid very little attention to it. Such an arrangement would be a jug-handled bargain indeed. The people of Canada were expected to guarantee dividends thus giving an absolutely safe investment to the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway and further allowing them, without taking any risk whatever, the risk being taken by the Canadian people, to share equally with the government any remaining profits. Such a suggestion was no compliment either to the Canadian people or to the Canadian parliament.

May I refer briefly to a recommendation made by the committee on the National railways during the last two sessions? That recommendation had to do with the writing down of the capitalization of the Canadian National Railways, something which I think the government should consider most seriously as soon as possible. The National railways are burdened with a much higher capitalization than they should carry as a business proposition under public ownership. That tremendous capitalization or, rather, over-capitalization, is the direct result of the failure of private ownership. It is therefore unfair to the Canadian National Railways as a public system that they should be burdened in perpetuity with a load which was left to them as a heritage from the failure of private ownership. The amount of indebtedness owing by the railways to the general public, the bondholders, is about $913,000,000. My figures may be a little astray, as they are not quite up to date, but I do not think that they are far out. The interest on that" debt amounts to some $38,000,000. Besides this, there is owing to the government of Canada a sum of $690,000,000 upon which there is interest amounting to $31,000,000. It has been suggested that it would be fair, to write off the amount of indebtedness owing by the National railways to the Canadian government and to confine the capital on which the railways might be expected to earn a fair return to the amount of indebtedness owing to the general public of some $900,000,000.

I want to deal briefly now with two or three outstanding features of the budget. It has been described as a Robb budget, as a popular budget, and as the people's budget. I believe it is a popular budget, and I imagine that my hon. friends opposite believe this also, although they might not ascribe the same reasons for its popularity as do hon. members on this side. It is a popular budget because for one thing it immediately touches the packets df everyone in Canada, and that is always a cogent argument everywhere.

speechtext:
When the hon. member
says that it touches the pockets of nearly all of the people, what does he mean?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, it does not take so
much out of their pockets as was taken before. What I have reference to is the reduction -in taxation. I shall come to that later. I presume it is not possible for a government to bring down a budget that would be entirely satisfactory to everyone, even if there were no such thing as party politics. I approve strongly of a good many things that are in the budget-and I have not always approved of budgets brought down in this House. Ever since the introduction of the stamp taxes I have opposed them. The stamp taxes have been properly described as nuisance taxes, and last year when the Minister of Finance abolished the stamp tax on cheques on sums of $5 and under, he took a step in the right direction, which was appreciated. This year he has wiped out the tax on receipts and that is a further step towards a better condition. I hope that he will continue the good work, and in another budget wipe out these taxes entirely.
The people are glad to see a reduction in postage to two cents. A good many of our friends opposite seek to minimize the importance of that reduction by suggesting that the cost of ordinary postage might well have remained at three cents and that the additional *revenue might have been applied to the
extension of" rural delivery. Now I should not like to put any obstacle in the way of serving the farmers and rural residents better in the matter of mail delivery, but I want to caution the government that this is perhaps one of the most costly services we have in Canada, a service the cost of which probably is perfectly justifiable. In my opinion, however, the rates charged for a public service ought to bear some definite relationship to the cost of that service, and I would no more blindly recommend a suggestion of the kind made than I would the granting of a subsidy by way of giving lower freight rates to any one section of the country at the expense of another.
